However, embedding advertisements within unstructured LLM outputs introduces a critical trilemma: balancing advertiser payoffs, platform revenue, and user experience. Existing methods, such as prompt injection or rigid position slots, disrupt semantic coherence and lack a parametric framework for independent control, rendering rigorous mechanism design intractable. To bridge this gap, we introduce Neuron Auctions, a novel paradigm that shifts the auction object from the surface text space to the LLM's internal representations. Leveraging mechanistic interpretability, we identify brand-specific feed-forward network (FFN) neurons and demonstrate that competing brands activate within approximately orthogonal subspaces. This near-perfect independence allows us to define continuous, disentangled intervention budgets (specifically, neuron counts and amplification factors) as auctionable commodities. Building on this computational carrier, we design a continuous menu-based auction mechanism that naturally guarantees strategy-proofness and optimizes revenue for the platform. By explicitly incorporating a user utility penalty into the platform's optimization objective, our framework dynamically prices out overly aggressive interventions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Neuron Auctions effectively preserve natural discourse quality while achieving an optimal alignment between commercial incentives and user satisfaction.

title: Management Consulting in the Artificial Intelligence – LLM Era
abstract: Management Consulting is one of the oldest and most well-established professional services across the world. Consultants have developed subject matter expertise and competency in a variety of areas such as General and Strategic Management, Financial Management, Marketing & Distribution Management, e-Business, Operations Management, Human Resource Management, Knowledge Management, Enterprise Performance Management, Business Transformation, Quality Management, and Information Technology. Information Technology as a discipline has evolved rapidly in the last three decades with software development paradigms and the advancement in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies. The space of AI & ML technologies is rapidly evolving, impacting the way insights are arrived at, how decisions are taken, organization models, and organization structures. This article explores the challenges, new opportunities and potential changes to the ways of working for management consultants given the developments in AI, particularly with large language models.
keywords: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

title: Large Language Models for Generative Recommendation: A Survey and Visionary Discussions
abstract: Large language models (LLM) not only have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP) but also have the potential to reshape many other fields, e.g., recommender systems (RS).However, most of the related work treats an LLM as a component of the conventional recommendation pipeline (e.g., as a feature extractor), which may not be able to fully leverage the generative power of LLM.Instead of separating the recommendation process into multiple stages, such as score computation and re-ranking, this process can be simplified to one stage with LLM: directly generating recommendations from the complete pool of items.This survey reviews the progress, methods, and future directions of LLM-based generative recommendation by examining three questions: 1) What generative recommendation is, 2) Why RS should advance to generative recommendation, and 3) How to implement LLM-based generative recommendation for various RS tasks.We hope that this survey can provide the context and guidance needed to explore this interesting and emerging topic.

title: Findings of the WMT24 General Machine Translation Shared Task: The LLM Era Is Here but MT Is Not Solved Yet
abstract: Tom Kocmi, Eleftherios Avramidis, Rachel Bawden, Ondřej Bojar, Anton Dvorkovich, Christian Federmann, Mark Fishel, Markus Freitag, Thamme Gowda, Roman Grundkiewicz, Barry Haddow, Marzena Karpinska, Philipp Koehn, Benjamin Marie, Christof Monz, Kenton Murray, Masaaki Nagata, Martin Popel, Maja Popović, Mariya Shmatova, Steinthór Steingrímsson, Vilém Zouhar. Proceedings of the Ninth Conference on Machine Translation. 2024.

title: Can LLMs Convert Graphs to Text-Attributed Graphs?
abstract: Graphs are ubiquitous structures found in numerous real-world applications, such as drug discovery, recommender systems, and social network analysis. To model graph-structured data, graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a popular tool. However, existing GNN architectures encounter challenges in cross-graph learning where multiple graphs have different feature spaces. To address this, recent approaches introduce text-attributed graphs (TAGs), where each node is associated with a textual description, which can be projected into a unified feature space using textual encoders. While promising, this method relies heavily on the availability of text-attributed graph data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel method named Topology-Aware Node description Synthesis (TANS), leveraging large language models (LLMs) to convert existing graphs into text-attributed graphs. The key idea is to integrate topological information into LLMs to explain how graph topology influences node semantics. We evaluate our TANS on text-rich, text-limited, and text-free graphs, demonstrating its applicability. Notably, on text-free graphs, our method significantly outperforms existing approaches that manually design node features, showcasing the potential of LLMs for preprocessing graph-structured data in the absence of textual information. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Zehong-Wang/TANS.
venue: Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (NAACL-HLT)

title: Evaluating Brand Retrieval and Ranking in Large Language Model Recommendations
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for product recommendation, but evaluating their recommendations presents challenges that differ from conventional information retrieval and recommender systems. LLMs can generate recommendations without an explicit candidate set, and repeated responses to the same query can produce different brands and rankings. We introduce a framework for evaluating open-ended LLM brand recommendations that defines the competitive set independently of model outputs and estimates recommendation prevalence and prominence through repeated sampling. We operationalize these constructs using Brand Recommendation Probability (BRP@$k$) and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR@$k$), and apply the framework to six LLMs across five product categories. Category-only queries reveal substantial omission of established brands and limited evidence that recommendation prominence follows conventional brand popularity. Instead, prominence is associated with broader marketplace-visibility signals, particularly search interest and online brand conversation. Needs-based queries show that contextualizing users' goals and constraints changes which brands are retrieved, while diagnostic positioning probes demonstrate that brands omitted from ordinary recommendations can remain conditionally retrievable when distinctive cues are supplied. These findings highlight the need to evaluate LLM recommendation as a stochastic retrieval-and-ranking process rather than from individual generated lists. We provide open-source software and data to support reproducible evaluation of LLM-generated brand recommendations.

title: General-Purpose Models for the Chemical Sciences: LLMs and Beyond
abstract: Data-driven techniques have a large potential to transform and accelerate the chemical sciences. However, chemical sciences also pose the unique challenge of very diverse, small, fuzzy data sets that are difficult to leverage in conventional machine learning approaches. A new class of models, which can be summarized under the term general-purpose models (GPMs) such as large language models, has shown the ability to solve tasks they have not been directly trained on, and to flexibly operate with low amounts of data in different formats. In this review, we discuss the fundamental building principles of GPMs and review recent and emerging applications of those models in the chemical sciences. While many of these applications are still in the prototype phase, we expect that the increasing interest in GPMs will make many of them mature in the coming years.

title: RTBAgent: A LLM-based Agent System for Real-Time Bidding
abstract: Real-Time Bidding (RTB) enables advertisers to place competitive bids on impression opportunities instantaneously, striving for cost-effectiveness in a highly competitive landscape. Although RTB has widely benefited from the utilization of technologies such as deep learning and reinforcement learning, the reliability of related methods often encounters challenges due to the discrepancies between online and offline environments and the rapid fluctuations of online bidding. To handle these challenges, RTBAgent is proposed as the first RTB agent system based on large language models (LLMs), which synchronizes real competitive advertising bidding environments and obtains bidding prices through an integrated decision-making process. Specifically, obtaining reasoning ability through LLMs, RTBAgent is further tailored to be more professional for RTB via involved auxiliary modules, i.e., click-through rate estimation model, expert strategy knowledge, and daily reflection. In addition, we propose a two-step decision-making process and multi-memory retrieval mechanism, which enables RTBAgent to review historical decisions and transaction records and subsequently make decisions more adaptive to market changes in real-time bidding. Empirical testing with real advertising datasets demonstrates that RTBAgent significantly enhances profitability. The RTBAgent code will be publicly accessible at: https://github.com/CaiLeng/RTBAgent.

title: Towards Open-World Recommendation with Knowledge Augmentation from Large Language Models
abstract: Recommender system plays a vital role in various online services. However, its insulated nature of training and deploying separately within a specific closed domain limits its access to open-world knowledge. Recently, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in bridging this gap by encoding extensive world knowledge and demonstrating reasoning capabilities. Nevertheless, previous attempts to directly use LLMs as recommenders cannot meet the inference latency demand of industrial recommender systems. In this work, we propose an Open-World Knowledge Augmented Recommendation Framework with Large Language Models, dubbed KAR, to acquire two types of external knowledge from LLMs — the reasoning knowledge on user preferences and the factual knowledge on items. We introduce factorization prompting to elicit accurate reasoning on user preferences. The generated reasoning and factual knowledge are effectively transformed and condensed into augmented vectors by a hybrid-expert adaptor in order to be compatible with the recommendation task. The obtained vectors can then be directly used to enhance the performance of any recommendation model. We also ensure efficient inference by preprocessing and prestoring the knowledge from the LLM. Extensive experiments show that KAR significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines and is compatible with a wide range of recommendation algorithms. We deploy KAR to Huawei’s news and music recommendation platforms and gain a 7% and 1.7% improvement in the online A/B test, respectively.

title: What is Your Data Worth to GPT? LLM-Scale Data Valuation with Influence Functions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on a vast amount of human-written data, but data providers often remain uncredited. In response to this issue, data valuation (or data attribution), which quantifies the contribution or value of each data to the model output, has been discussed as a potential solution. Nevertheless, applying existing data valuation methods to recent LLMs and their vast training datasets has been largely limited by prohibitive compute and memory costs. In this work, we focus on influence functions, a popular gradient-based data valuation method, and significantly improve its scalability with an efficient gradient projection strategy called LoGra that leverages the gradient structure in backpropagation. We then provide a theoretical motivation of gradient projection approaches to influence functions to promote trust in the data valuation process. Lastly, we lower the barrier to implementing data valuation systems by introducing LogIX, a software package that can transform existing training code into data valuation code with minimal effort. In our data valuation experiments, LoGra achieves competitive accuracy against more expensive baselines while showing up to 6,500x improvement in throughput and 5x reduction in GPU memory usage when applied to Llama3-8B-Instruct and the 1B-token dataset.

title: Auto prompting without training labels: An LLM cascade for product quality assessment in e-commerce catalogs
abstract: We introduce a novel, training free cascade for auto-prompting Large Language Models (LLMs) to assess product quality in e-commerce. Our system requires no training labels or model fine-tuning, instead automatically generating and refining prompts for evaluating attribute quality across tens of thousands of product category–attribute pairs. Starting from a seed of human-crafted prompts, the cascade progressively optimizes instructions to meet catalog-specific requirements. This approach bridges the gap between general language understanding and domain-specific knowledge at scale in complex industrial catalogs. Our extensive empirical evaluations shows the auto-prompt cascade improves precision and recall by 8–10% over traditional chain-of-thought prompting. Notably, it achieves these gains while reducing domain expert effort from 5.1 hours to 3 minutes per attribute - a 99% reduction. Additionally, the cascade generalizes effectively across five languages and multiple quality assessment tasks, consistently maintaining performance gains.
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)

title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling
abstract: The reasoning capabilities of the recent LLMs enable them to execute external function calls to overcome their inherent limitations, such as knowledge cutoffs, poor arithmetic skills, or lack of access to private data. This development has allowed LLMs to select and coordinate multiple functions based on the context to tackle more complex problems. However, current methods for function calling often require sequential reasoning and acting for each function which can result in high latency, cost, and sometimes inaccurate behavior. To address this, we introduce LLMCompiler, which executes functions in parallel to efficiently orchestrate multiple function calls. Drawing inspiration from the principles of classical compilers, LLMCompiler enables parallel function calling with three components: (i) a Function Calling Planner, formulating execution plans for function calling; (ii) a Task Fetching Unit, dispatching function calling tasks; and (iii) an Executor, executing these tasks in parallel. LLMCompiler automatically generates an optimized orchestration for the function calls and can be used with both open-source and closed-source models. We have benchmarked LLMCompiler on a range of tasks with different patterns of function calling. We observe consistent latency speedup of up to 3.7x, cost savings of up to 6.7x, and accuracy improvement of up to ~9% compared to ReAct. Our code is available at https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler.

title: BoolXLLM: LLM-Assisted Explainability for Boolean Models
abstract: Interpretable machine learning aims to provide transparent models whose decision-making processes can be readily understood by humans. Recent advances in rule-based approaches, such as expressive Boolean formulas (BoolXAI), offer faithful and compact representations of model behavior. However, for non-technical stakeholders, main challenges remain in practice: (i) selecting semantically meaningful features and (ii) translating formal logical rules into accessible explanations. In this work, we propose BoolXLLM , as a hybrid framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) into the end-to-end pipeline of Boolean rule learning. We augment BoolXAI , an expressive Boolean rule-based classifier, with LLMs at three critical stages: (1) feature selection, where LLMs guide the identification of domain-relevant variables; (2) threshold recommendation, where LLMs propose semantically meaningful discretization strategies for numerical features; and (3) rule compression and interpretation, where Boolean rules are translated into natural language explanations at both global and local levels. This integration bridges formal, faithful explanations with human-understandable narratives. This allows build an explainable AI system that is both theoretically grounded and accessible to non-experts. Early empirical results demonstrate that LLM-assisted pipelines improve interpretability while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our work highlights the promise of combining symbolic reasoning with language-based models for human-centered explainability.

title: Efficiency Unleashed: Inference Acceleration for LLM-based Recommender Systems with Speculative Decoding
abstract: The past few years have witnessed a growing interest in LLM-based recommender systems (RSs), although their industrial deployment remains in a preliminary stage. Most existing deployments leverage LLMs offline as feature enhancers, generating augmented knowledge for downstream tasks. However, in recommendation scenarios with numerous users and items, even offline knowledge generation with LLMs demands significant time and computational resources. This inefficiency arises from the autoregressive nature of LLMs. A promising solution is speculative decoding, a Draft-Then-Verify approach that increases the number of tokens generated per decoding step. In this work, we first identify recommendation knowledge generation as a highly fitting use case for retrieval-based speculative decoding. Then, we discern its two characteristics: (1) the vast number of items and users in RSs leads to retrieval inefficiency, and (2) RSs exhibit high diversity tolerance for LLM-generated text. Building on these insights, we introduce Lossless Acceleration via Speculative Decoding for LLM-based Recommender Systems (LASER), which features a Customized Retrieval Pool to enhance retrieval efficiency and Relaxed Verification to improve the acceptance rate of draft tokens. LASER achieves a 3-5x speedup on public datasets and saves about 67% of computational resources during the online A/B test on a large-scale advertising scenario with lossless downstream recommendation performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/YunjiaXi/LASER
venue: International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)

title: Consumer AI as Health Plan Decision Support A Benchmark of LLM Plan Recommendations against a Claims-based Pricing Engine
keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

title: Adaptive Generation of Bias-Eliciting Questions for LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely deployed in user-facing applications, reaching hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Despite their widespread adoption, growing reliance on their outputs raises significant concerns, particularly as users may be exposed to model-inherent biases that disadvantage or stereotype certain groups. However, existing bias benchmarks commonly rely on simple templated prompts or restrictive multiple-choice questions that fail to capture the complexity of real-world user interactions. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a counterfactual framework that automatically generates realistic, open-ended questions for LLM bias evaluation. Through iterative question mutation, our approach systematically explores areas where models are most likely to exhibit biased behavior. Beyond just detecting harmful biases, we also capture increasingly relevant response dimensions, such as asymmetric refusals and explicit bias acknowledgment. Building on this, we construct CAB, a diverse and human-verified benchmark for realistic and nuanced bias evaluations on current frontier LLMs. Our evaluation using CAB highlights the continued need for fairness research by showing that all examined models exhibit persistent biases across certain scenarios.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Mechanism Design for Quality-Preserving LLM Advertising
abstract: Embedding advertisements into large language model (LLM) outputs introduces a fundamental tension: revenue optimization can distort content and degrade user experience. Existing approaches largely ignore this trade-off, often forcing irrelevant ads into responses. We propose a quality-preserving auction framework that explicitly integrates content fidelity into the mechanism design. Built on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), our approach treats organic content as a reference and derives an endogenous reserve price that screens out ads with non-positive marginal social welfare contributions. We develop a KL-regularized single-allocation mechanism with Myerson payments and a screened VCG multi-allocation mechanism, both satisfying dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and individual rationality. Experiments across diverse scenarios demonstrate that our mechanisms outperform existing baselines in metrics such as revenue per ad and semantic similarity to no-ad responses. Our results establish a new paradigm for LLM advertising that enables monetization without compromising output quality.

title: The Price of Transparency: How Generative AI Advertising Disclosure Affects Consumer Purchase Intention
abstract: This dataset supports the findings of the study titled "The Price of Transparency: How Generative AI Advertising Disclosure Affects Consumer Purchase Intention" The dataset includes six files: advertisement stimuli used in the pre-study for stimulus selection, raw data collected from 20 participants in the pre-study, the survey instrument containing all measurement items, raw data from the AI-disclosed condition, raw data from the AI-undisclosed condition, and SPSS result. All data were collected from Indonesian respondents via online survey using a between-subjects experimental design grounded in the Persuasion Knowledge Model (PKM).
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Effects of Generative AI Advertising Disclosure on Brand Authenticity Perceptions Purchase Intention and Consumer Skepticism Among Generation Z Consumers
abstract: The increasing application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital advertising has introduced substantial changes in how brands develop promotional content, communicate product information, and establish relationships with consumers. However, explicitly disclosing AI involvement in advertisement production may influence perceived brand authenticity, purchase intention, and consumer skepticism, particularly among Generation Z consumers who demonstrate considerable familiarity with digitally mediated brand communication. This study proposes an integrated computational and behavioural framework for investigating the direct, indirect, and conditional effects of generative AI advertising disclosure on consumer responses. A novel Disclosure–Authenticity–Skepticism Predictive Model (DASPM) is developed to quantify how disclosure characteristics, including disclosure visibility, specificity, timing, and perceived transparency, influence brand authenticity perceptions and purchase intention through consumer skepticism. The proposed framework integrates structural equation modelling (SEM), moderated mediation analysis, and machine learning techniques to examine both theoretically specified causal pathways and complex predictive relationships. A randomized experimental survey involving Generation Z consumers aged 18–29 years is proposed, using matched advertisements assigned to three conditions: undisclosed AI-generated advertising, explicitly disclosed AI-generated advertising, and human-created advertising. Brand authenticity, consumer skepticism, advertising credibility, AI familiarity, and purchase intention are measured using validated multi-item Likert scales. The DASPM framework incorporates latent-variable estimation, interaction effects, nonlinear feature transformations, and predictive modelling, with its performance evaluated against conventional multiple linear regression, partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Comparative evaluation will employ coefficient of determination (R²), root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and cross-validated predictive performance, alongside bootstrapped indirect-effect estimates and measurement validity assessments. The results section is designed to present comparative performance graphs, conditional indirect-effect plots, disclosure-treatment comparisons, and feature-importance analyses to determine whether transparent AI disclosure strengthens consumer trust or activates skepticism that reduces purchase intention. The study will also investigate whether perceived brand authenticity mediates the disclosure–purchase intention relationship and whether AI literacy and prior brand familiarity moderate these effects. The proposed framework is intended to advance understanding of generative AI advertising disclosure by combining experimental consumer research with interpretable predictive analytics, providing an evidence-based approach to evaluating disclosure strategies and their implications for brand communication among Generation Z consumers.
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Humanities and Social Sciences
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Generative AI in Advertising: Balancing Business Efficiency and Consumer Trust
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly changed the way businesses can create advertisements by providing custom content for a low cost. However, the use of generative AI has increasingly begun to raise questions about creativity and transparency; for businesses, the use of generative AI has also begun to spark dilemmas involving consumer trust, and the role of humans within advertising. This literature review examines how generative AI affects advertising from both a business and consumer perspective. Existing research was analyzed through AI disclosure, perceived authenticity, creativity, purchase intention, traditional versus generative AI, and business efficiency. The literature generally suggests that consumers can respond negatively when it is revealed that an advertisement was generated by AI, especially when they already have preconceived notions of generative AI being unauthentic or low effort. Nevertheless, recent research has also demonstrated generative AI can also boost engagement by increasing perceptions of novelty, when the audience views generative AI positively. The stark contrast between these findings suggest that consumer responses cannot be determined solely based on whether or not AI was used, but by the nuances of its use: the type of product being advertised, the transparency of the advertisement, and the opinions of the target audience are factors that all influence advertising outcomes. As a whole, generative AI can provide significant opportunities to businesses to reduce cost and increase the scale of advertisement production, but companies must balance these advantages with the concerns regarding consumer expectations for authenticity and creativity.
venue: Student Journal of Business and Economics

title: Service ads in the era of generative AI: Disclosures, trust, and intangibility
venue: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services

title: Consumer Attitudes Toward AI-Generated Advertising: Focusing on the Moderating Effects of AI Literacy and AI Disclosure
abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into advertising is reshaping marketing practices, with AI-generated advertisements gaining prominence as a novel trend. Despite this growth, consumer responses remain ambivalent, characterized by persistent biases and heterogeneous acceptance levels that constrain advertising effectiveness. This study explores how attitudes toward traditional versus AI-generated advertisements differ, while also assessing the moderating roles of AI literacy and AI disclosure. Two controlled experiments were conducted. Findings from Experiment 1 reveal that consumers consistently evaluated traditional advertisements more favorably, irrespective of whether ad type was accurately disclosed. Results from Experiment 2 further reveal that individuals with high AI literacy evaluated AI-generated ads more positively and were less sensitive to AI disclosure, whereas those with low AI literacy exhibited broadly negative responses. These results demonstrate the conditional influence of AI literacy on the acceptance of AI-driven advertising, offering new insights for theory development and practical guidance for designing effective AI-based advertising strategies.
venue: The Journal of Internet Electronic Commerce Resarch

title: “Made with AI” but why? How consumers interpret beneficiary-framed AI disclosures in advertising
abstract: As generative AI becomes more prevalent in advertising, firms increasingly face requirements to disclose AI involvement. Although prior research shows that such disclosures may generate negative consumer responses, it remains unclear whether explanatory disclosures can mitigate these effects. This research examines beneficiary-framed AI disclosures, explanations communicating why AI was used and who benefits, across three studies. In a controlled text-based experiment (Study 1), more specific explanations improve evaluations relative to minimal and less specific AI labels. However, beneficiary framing effects are not systematic, and practically negligible. Moreover, these benefits do not generalize to more realistic advertising contexts. Across two Instagram-style ad studies (Studies 2A and 2B), explanatory disclosures fail to improve consumer responses and, in some cases, lead to more negative evaluations with effects that are either statistically equivalent to zero or significantly negative. Across studies, AI aversion emerges as a robust predictor of negative responses, suggesting that disclosure effects are driven more by consumers’ prior beliefs than by the specific framing of explanations. The findings suggest caution in adding explanatory disclosures, as default inferences of firm-serving motives are difficult to override.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Investigating the Impact of Disclosing Generative AI’s Involvement in Video Advertising
abstract: The deployment of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in advertising industry has witnessed a significant increase during recent years. However, consensus on whether consumers should be informed of generative AI’s involvement in video advertisement creation and how to mitigate the potential negative effects caused by such disclosure has not been well investigated. Drawing upon signaling theory, this research aims to investigate the effect caused by generative AI involvement disclosure in video advertisement. Besides, we provide possible explanation by examining the mediating role of authenticity perception. In addition, we suggest that the potential negative effects caused by AI involvement disclosure could be alleviated by adjusting the timing of disclosure. In this paper, we will discuss three experimental studies with the aim of testing the direct effects, the possible explanation, and the effects of timing strategy. This research will contribute to both theory development and the practice of AI deployment and human-AI collaboration within advertising field.
venue: Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS)

title: Trust and Deception in AI-Generated Advertising: The Double-Edged Role of AI Realism, Disclosure, and Consumer AI Literacy
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is blurring the boundary between human-made and machine-generated communication. As AI-generated content becomes increasingly realistic, audiences must evaluate not only what a message communicates but also how and by whom it was produced. This study examines how perceived AI realism shapes trust and deception judgments in AI-generated advertising and whether these effects depend on AI disclosure and consumers' AI literacy. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 224 adult consumers. AI realism (high vs. low) and AI disclosure (disclosed vs. undisclosed) were manipulated in a 2 x 2 experimental design, while AI literacy was treated as a measured continuous moderator. Participants viewed an AI-generated advertisement for a fictitious dietary supplement brand and evaluated advertising trust, brand trust, and perceived deception. Conditional process analyses using PROCESS Macro Model 3 were conducted with gender and age as control variables. The findings reveal a double-edged role of AI realism. Higher AI realism increased advertising trust and brand trust across experimental conditions. Disclosure strengthened the trust-enhancing effect of AI realism, while AI literacy further shaped this effect only for brand trust. For perceived deception, higher AI realism increased deception judgments most strongly when AI use was not disclosed. When disclosure was provided, conditional probing showed that this deception-enhancing effect weakened and was not significant at higher levels of AI literacy, although the three-way interaction was not statistically significant. These results show that AI realism is not merely a positive cue of content quality. Rather, its effects depend on transparency practices and consumers' interpretive competence regarding AI-generated content.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Technology Anxiety and Brand Trust: Consumer Responses to Generative-AI Advertising
abstract: This structured integrative review examines how consumers interpret generative-AI advertising and how those interpretations shape brand trust. The review synthesizes 21 studies published between 2018 and 2025 across six evidence domains: AI advertising, AI disclosure, algorithm aversion, personalization and privacy, AI agents, and virtual influencers. Sixteen sources are primary empirical studies, three are reviews or meta-analyses, and two are conceptual articles. The analysis organizes the evidence through an extended Stimulus-Organism-Response framework. GenAI advertising cues, including disclosure, personalization, data-use transparency, human oversight, and human-likeness, are treated as stimuli. Consumers form parallel threat appraisals, such as technology anxiety, privacy concern, autonomy loss, perceived risk, and inauthenticity, and benefit or relational appraisals, such as authenticity, credibility, competence, social presence, control, and perceived agency. Brand trust is positioned as the proximal relational state that links these appraisals to approach outcomes, including ad attitude, engagement, purchase intention, data disclosure, and positive word of mouth, as well as avoidance outcomes. The synthesis indicates that AI disclosure is not intrinsically harmful or beneficial: outcomes depend on task subjectivity, data sensitivity, explanation quality, responsible brand conduct, and consumer capabilities. The article contributes a parsimonious S-O-R framework, an evidence-domain profile of the literature, and propositions that can guide future experiments and survey-based SEM in Vietnam.
venue: Pancasila International Journal of Applied Social Science
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Creativity Under Disclosure: How AI Disclosure Labels Shape Consumers’ Perceptions of Advertising Creativity
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in advertising has transformed creative production while simultaneously raising concerns about transparency, authenticity and consumer perception. With the growing integration of GenAI into advertising, understanding how consumers respond to AI disclosure has become increasingly important. This study investigates how AI disclosure in advertising influences consumers’ perceptions of creativity and examines whether originality, appropriateness and skepticism mediate this relationship. Drawing on the Persuasion Knowledge Model, algorithmic aversion theory and advertising creativity literature, a quantitative online survey using a between-subject experimental design was conducted. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure or no-disclosure condition while evaluating the same advertisement. Data were analyzed using independent samples t-tests and mediation analyses. The findings show that AI disclosure significantly reduces advertising creativity. Advertisements labeled as AI-generated were evaluated as less creative than identical advertisements without disclosure. The results further demonstrate that this effect is primarily driven by lower perceptions of originality and appropriateness. While AI disclosure slightly increased skepticism, skepticism did not significantly mediate the relationship between disclosure and creativity. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-generated advertising by positioning perceived creativity as a central outcome variable in AI disclosure contexts. The findings further highlight the challenges marketers face in balancing transparency requirements with maintaining the creative impact of advertising campaigns.
venue: Lund University Publications Student Papers (Lund University)

title: Trust Issues: AI Advertising Edition : A qualitative study of how advertising elements and AI disclosure levels influence perceived advertising credibility among consumers.
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has transformed how commercials are created and communicated to consumers. While AI-generated advertising offers advantages such as efficiency, scalability, and lower production costs, it also raises questions regarding authenticity, trust, and perceived advertising credibility. This study examines how advertising elements and disclosure levels in AI-generated commercials influence consumers perceived advertising credibility. A qualitative research approach was applied through semi-structured interviews with nine participants between the ages of 18 and 30 who regularly use AI technologies. Participants viewed two AI-generated commercials with different advertising styles and disclosure strategies before discussing their perceptions of credibility, authenticity, realism, emotional connection, and trustworthiness. The collected material was analysed through thematic analysis. The findings show that perceived advertising credibility in AI-generated commercials is shaped by the interaction between advertising elements and disclosure framing. Visual realism, relatable storytelling, human-like voice design, and coherent messaging contributed positively to credibility when the commercial appeared authentic, sincere, and believable. In contrast, exaggerated visuals, artificial emotional expression, robotic audio, and unclear messaging reduced credibility by making AI involvement more visible and weakening perceptions of human presence. Fully AI-generated disclosure often increased skepticism, particularly when the advertisement already appeared artificial or lacked human involvement. Human-supervised and AI-assisted framing reduced negative reactions by signalling responsibility, effort, and human control. The study concludes that credibility in AI-generated commercials is not determined solely by whether AI is used, but by how AI involvement is communicated and how successfully the advertising elements create perceptions of authenticity, sincerity, and human presence. The findings contribute to a broader understanding of consumer perceptions of AI-generated advertising and offer practical insights for organisations seeking to use AI in advertising while maintaining consumer trust and credibility.

title: Timing of AI Disclosure in Promotional Video Advertising : An Experimental Study of Consumer Trust, Attitude and Scepticism
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into advertising production, questions surrounding transparency and consumer responses to AI disclosure have become more important. Prior research shows that AI disclosure can influence advertising evaluations, but existing studies have mainly examined disclosure as a present-or-absent condition, often in static advertising formats. Less attention has been given to whether the timing of disclosure matters, particularly in promotional video advertising where the message unfolds sequentially over time. This study examines how the timing of AI disclosure influences consumers’ trust, attitude and scepticism towards AI-generated promotional video content. Drawing on disclosure timing research, with the Persuasion Knowledge Model used as a supporting theoretical framework, the study compares three experimental conditions: no disclosure, pre-exposure disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 239 participants, who were exposed to one version of an AI-generated promotional video before completing a structured questionnaire. The findings did not reveal statistically significant differences between the disclosure conditions for trust, attitude or scepticism. However, the descriptive results followed a consistent directional pattern, with pre-exposure disclosure associated with slightly lower trust and attitude and slightly higher scepticism than both no disclosure and post-exposure disclosure. Exploratory analyses further suggested that participants’ familiarity with generative AI and their broader attitudes towards AI-generated video content may be relevant contextual factors influencing consumer evaluations. The study contributes to AI disclosure research by conceptualising disclosure as a temporally positioned cue within promotional video advertising. It suggests that disclosure timing may be theoretically meaningful, but that timing alone may be insufficient to produce strong immediate effects on consumer evaluation.

title: The Influence of Brand Credibility on the Perception of Advertising Created by Generative AI
abstract: This master's thesis focuses on the role of brand credibility in consumers' perception of advertising created by generative artificial intelligence. Although consumer responses to AI- generated advertising and the effect of its disclosure have been the subject of a number of previous studies, brand credibility as a distinct moderator of these responses has not yet been empirically tested. The aim of the thesis is to examine whether brand credibility influences the evaluation of advertising created by generative AI in the context of disclosing or not disclosing its origin, and whether the use of AI-generated advertising has a reverse effect on the perceived credibility of the brand. A total of five hypotheses were formulated, and to test them empirically, an online experiment with a mixed design was conducted, in which brand credibility was operationalised through descriptions of real and fictitious brands across four categories of low-involvement consumer goods, while the presence of an "AI-generated" disclosure label was varied between subjects. A total of 242 responses were analysed by means of a mixed analysis of variance and correlation analyses. Of the five hypotheses, only the first was supported: advertising of a credible brand was evaluated more favourably than advertising of a...
venue: Digital Repository (National Repository of Grey Literature)
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: The Dark Side of Generative AI in Marketing: AI-Generated False and Misleading Advertising and Its Consumer Consequences
abstract: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling marketers to create persuasive text, images, and other promotional content rapidly and at lower cost. At the same time, the ability of generative systems to produce highly realistic content creates concerns about deception, misinformation, transparency, and the credibility of consumer-facing information. The present study examines the consumer consequences of AI-generated false and misleading advertising, with particular emphasis on hallucinated product claims. The study focuses on whether AI-generated hallucinated product claims influence perceived deception, AI skepticism, and perceived information reliability, and whether these consumer responses subsequently shape purchase intention. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) framework, the study conceptualizes hallucinated product claims as the stimulus, the three consumer evaluations as the organism, and purchase intention as the response. A quantitative, cross-sectional, deductive research design was adopted. Data were collected from 320 business-school students and faculty members through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and the model was assessed using SmartPLS. The reported measurement results show Cronbach's alpha values above 0.70, composite reliability above the stated threshold, and average variance extracted above 0.50 for all constructs, indicating acceptable reliability and convergent validity. The reported discriminant-validity matrix also supports construct distinctiveness. The structural model reports a VIF range of 1.47-2.24 and an R² of 0.421 for purchase intention. Four of the six hypotheses are supported. AI-generated hallucinated product claims significantly increase perceived deception and significantly reduce perceived information reliability. Perceived deception significantly reduces purchase intention, while perceived information reliability significantly increases purchase intention. The paths from hallucinated product claims to AI skepticism and from AI skepticism to purchase intention are not statistically significant. The findings indicate that message-level judgments of deception and information reliability are more consequential for purchase intention in the reported model than generalized skepticism toward AI. The study extends the S-O-R perspective to the dark side of GenAI in advertising and highlights the importance of factual verification, transparency, human oversight, disclosure, and consumer AI literacy. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; AI hallucinations; misleading advertising; perceived deception; AI skepticism; perceived information reliability; purchase intention; stimulus-organism-response theory.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Generative AI Disclosure in Fashion Marketing: A Tectonic Shift in the Advertising Landscape
abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has leveraged fashion marketing by enabling swift and efficient content creation. However, a research gap in understanding its acceptance from the perspective of a consumer viewing an AI-generated advertisement remains, while regulations begin to make disclosure mandatory. As generative AI is envisioned to bring immense innovation to marketing methods, a between-subject experimental study was developed to test the effects of AI-generated advertisement disclosure on consumer affective states and thus motivational outcomes. Evidence shows that while negative perception regarding AI-generated content was prevalent, perceived effort and brand attitude hold potential to alleviate the detrimental effects of AI-generated image disclosure, without provoking consumers’ perceived risk. Findings show managerial implications for the future of AI-generated content in fashion marketing.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: AI-generated versus human-created advertising: Effects on consumer trust and purchase intent
abstract: Research background: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has profoundly influenced the marketing landscape, particularly advertising practices. Despite significant growth and widespread integration of AI-generated content, consumer reactions toward explicit disclosure of AI involvement remain uncertain. Previous studies indicate that while AI-generated advertisements can enhance efficiency and personalisation, they may negatively affect consumer perceptions of authenticity and credibility. However, the role of disclosure ("created by AI" vs. "created by human") and product involvement level (high vs. low involvement) as moderators of consumer trust and purchase intentions remains under-explored. Purpose of the article: The purpose of this research is to empirically investigate how advertisement generation source (AI vs. human) combined with explicit labelling influences consumer trust and purchase intent, while also considering product involvement as a moderating factor. Methods: The study employed a 2 (ad generation source: AI vs. human) × 2 (ad labelling: labelled as AI vs. labelled as human) between-subjects experimental design. Participants were randomly assigned to four conditions, assessing advertisements for both low-involvement (snacks) and high-involvement products (laptops). Consumer trust and purchase intent were measured across multiple validated dimensions. Data analysis included one-way ANOVA and Tukey post-hoc tests to identify significant group differences. Findings & value added: The results confirm significant differences in consumer trust and purchase intent based on advertisement generation source and labelling conditions, fully supporting all hypothesised effects. Specifically, advertisements labelled as human-generated received higher consumer trust and purchase intent ratings, even if they were AI-generated. Conversely, transparently labelled AI-generated ads caused lower trust and intent, particularly for high-involvement products. These findings reveal context-specific reactions to AI disclosures, underscore the importance of authenticity in digital marketing, and advise marketers to manage AI disclosures carefully to preserve trust and drive purchases.
venue: Equilibrium Quarterly Journal of Economics and Economic Policy

title: Disclaimer! This Content Is AI-Generated: How AI-Disclosures Influence Trust in Advertisements and Organizations
abstract: The use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) for advertising is raising issues around ethics and transparency. This type of AI adds an extra manipulative layer to advertisements because it makes it harder for consumers to determine whether elements of an ad are real or AI-generated. This study aims to explore the effect of AI disclosures in GAI-created advertisements on trust in the advertisement and the organization. Moreover, this study tests whether these effects can be explained by conceptual AI knowledge and attitudinal persuasion knowledge. A one-factorial (GAI advertisement with versus without disclosure) between-subjects design experiment was conducted (N = 304). The results showed that AI disclosures increased conceptual AI knowledge and attitudinal persuasion knowledge, resulting in a decrease in trust towards the advertisement and organization. However, a positive effect of AI disclosures was also found, whereby the disclosure increased attitudinal persuasion knowledge, which lead to an increase in trust.

title: Impact of Generative AI on Consumer Trust in Digital Advertising (focus on tools like Chat GPT) A Study in Thrissur District, Kerala
abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the landscape of digital advertising, enabling marketers to create highly personalized, scalable, and cost-efficient content. Tools such as Chat GPT allow the generation of human like advertising messages, raising critical concerns regarding consumer trust. Drawing on theories of consumer trust and technology acceptance, the research proposes a conceptual framework linking AI-generated content and consumer trust. The study also investigates the effects of AI disclosure and consumer AI literacy on these relationships. Respondents will be exposed to both AI-generated and human -created advertisements to assess differences in perception, followed by structured data collection. The research aims to investigate whether AI -generated advertisement enhance or undermine consumer trust and purchase intention.
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: THE IMPACT OF ADOPTING AND DISCLOSING GENERATIVE AI IN DIGITAL ADVERTISING ON BRAND PERCEPTIONS
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has significantly transformed digital advertising, enabling the automated creation of marketing content. However, concerns persist regarding its impact on brand perception, particularly in terms of brand love and authenticity. This study examines how the adoption and disclosure of GenAI-generated video advertisements influence consumer perceptions. Using a 2x2 between-subjects experimental design, the research investigates the interaction between GenAI adoption (AI-generated vs. human-created) and disclosure (label present vs. absent) on brand love, with brand authenticity as a potential mediator. Expected findings suggest that disclosing AI-generated content negatively affects brand love, while perceived brand authenticity may mitigate this effect. The study contributes to the literature on AI in branding and offers practical insights for marketers navigating the balance between technological innovation and brand trust in digital advertising.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: The effect of AI disclosure on perceived creativity and purchase intention in luxury advertising.
abstract: This study examines the impact of disclosing the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in luxury advertising on consumer perceptions and behavioral intentions. Specifically, it investigates whether informing consumers that an advertisement was generated using AI influences perceived creativity and purchase intention. The study is motivated by the increasing use of generative AI in marketing and the growing regulatory requirement for transparency regarding AI-generated content. While AI enables efficient content creation, luxury branding is traditionally associated with human craftsmanship, creativity, and authenticity, potentially creating tension when AI involvement is disclosed. The research employs a randomized between-subjects experimental design in which participants are assigned to either an AI disclosure condition or a no-disclosure condition. Participants are exposed to multiple luxury advertisements that are identical across conditions except for the presence of an AI disclosure label. The study tests whether AI disclosure negatively affects perceived effort and perceived creativity, and whether these effects translate into lower purchase intention through a serial mediation mechanism. Additionally, it examines whether these effects are moderated by individual differences in need for uniqueness. The findings are expected to contribute to research on AI in marketing and luxury consumption, and to provide practical insights for brands and policymakers regarding the consequences of AI disclosure in high-end markets.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: AI-Generated Advertising Content and Brand Authenticity: a Comparative Consumer Study
abstract: Generative AI now produces advertising copy, images and video at a fraction of the cost and time of human creative work, and the quality of its output is often indistinguishable from human-created content. What consumers make of it, once they know, is less clear. This paper examines perceived brand authenticity across three ad-creation conditions, human-created, AI-generated without disclosure and AI-generated with disclosure, in a comparative simulation of 1,200 consumers that also varies brand type. AI-generated content undisclosed lowers perceived authenticity modestly (0.65 to 0.59) despite slightly higher execution quality; disclosure lowers it substantially (to 0.43), and the penalty is larger for heritage brands (0.38) than for non-heritage brands (0.48). Brand attitude follows authenticity, so that disclosed AI content yields the lowest attitude despite the highest quality. The paper interprets the results through brand authenticity theory, in which authenticity rests on perceived genuineness, origin and craft, argues that AI generation threatens the origin and craft components in proportion to how central they are to the brand, and derives guidance on where AI content fits, how disclosure should be handled under emerging transparency requirements, and how brands can preserve authenticity while using generative tools.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: The Effects of AI Disclosure and Explanatory Transparency on Consumer Trust and Purchase Intention in E-commerce AI Advertising: A 2×2 Scenario Experiment
abstract: As generative AI becomes more common in advertising production, understanding how AI disclosure and explanatory transparency shape consumer responses has become increasingly important. The study used a 2 × 2 between-subjects online scenario experiment to examine how AI disclosure and explanatory transparency shaped trust and purchase intention in an e-commerce advertising context. A total of 122 responses were collected, with 90 valid cases retained for analysis. However, significant interaction effects were found for both dependent variables, suggesting that consumers did not respond to these cues independently. Instead, disclosure appeared to be understood differently depending on the explanation that accompanied it. The transparency manipulation check was not significant, so transparency-related findings should be interpreted with caution. Overall, the study suggests that consumers are more likely to evaluate AI-related advertising by reading disclosure and explanation together rather than as separate pieces of information. Future research could test these relationships with stronger transparency manipulations and more diverse samples.
venue: Advances in Social Science, Education and Humanities Research/Advances in social science, education and humanities research

title: Generative AI and Marketing Effectiveness: Balancing Efficiency, Consumer Trust, and Responsible Adoption
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the ways in which artificial intelligence (AI) adoption has transformed the marketing function and the advertising industry, as well as the conditions needed to ensure continued advertising effectiveness in a context where consumer attention is shrinking, and distrust of AI-generated content is on the rise. Specifically, it examines how generative AI is transforming marketing and advertising by reducing content-production costs while reshaping how consumers discover information, perceive brand communications, and respond to AI-generated content. It also aims to identify the conditions under which advertisers, agencies, and industry bodies can adopt generative AI responsibly while preserving consumer trust, creative quality, and marketing effectiveness. The study adopts a position-paper approach informed by more than 20 years of professional experience across advertising agencies, technology providers, and advertisers. It draws on contemporary industry research, regulatory developments, market data, and practitioner perspectives, including those of a leading industry association, and uses illustrative cases to assess the operational benefits, consumer implications, and governance requirements associated with generative AI in marketing. The article demonstrates that generative AI can substantially reduce production costs, accelerate creative execution, and support the increasing volume, localization, and operational management of marketing content. However, its widespread use also contributes to the commoditization of low-quality synthetic content, leading to growing consumer concern about misinformation. Search engines and social media platforms, where audiences spend most of their time online, have integrated AI into their operations to the point of changing search behavior and product discovery in the former case and enabling anyone to produce low-quality AI content in the latter. The article indicates that AI-generated advertising may be less effective than human-produced work at building brand and driving sales when content-production efficiency is prioritized over strategic insight, distinctive creativity, transparency, and emotional resonance. Advertisers and agencies should use AI to augment rather than replace human strategic and creative judgment. Responsible adoption requires transparent disclosure of synthetic content, robust governance and procurement standards, safeguards for data security and intellectual property, bias mitigation, attention to environmental impact, and workflows that direct efficiency gains toward stronger brand building and customer value. Industry associations and regulators can reinforce these practices through shared standards and clear guidance. As a position paper, this study relies on professional experience, selected industry evidence, published market data, and illustrative cases rather than original empirical testing. Because generative AI technologies, consumer behavior, platform practices, and regulation are evolving rapidly, some observations may require reassessment as the market develops. Further analysis is needed as more research data become available on the performance of AI-generated versus traditional content and on advertising effectiveness. Future research should test the proposed responsible-adoption principles across industries, markets, and consumer groups and propose new responsible-use guidelines where relevant. The study connects operational efficiency, consumer trust, advertising effectiveness, and responsible AI governance within a single marketing-focused analysis. It offers advertisers, agencies, industry associations, and policymakers a practical basis for adopting generative AI in ways that preserve transparency, content quality, human creativity, and audience receptivity, and that ultimately deliver continued advertising effectiveness and long-term brand impact.

title: Possibilities of Generative AI
abstract: This special issue focuses on generative AI, which has garnered significant attention in recent years, and explores its impact on business, particularly marketing, and its potential. History shows that technologies are shaped not by initial expectations, but through social practices. The five articles in this issue examine generative AI from multiple perspectives. Two studies address consumer behavior, emphasizing anthropomorphism and emotional AI in shaping advertising evaluations and self-disclosure in travel planning. Three further contributions turn to organizational and industry contexts: exploring AI-assisted programming and tacit knowledge transfer, the role of generative AI in human resource management, and transformations in marketing communications, including shifting power relations between brands, platforms, and consumers. Together, these studies demonstrate the diverse ways in which generative AI is being applied, perceived, and debated.

title: The AI-Generated Advertising Paradox: Content Authenticity, Consumer Skepticism, and Brand Credibility
abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has created a fundamental tension between production efficiency and consumer perceptions of authenticity. Although AI-generated advertising enables brands to produce promotional content rapidly, economically, and at scale, consumers may question whether such communication reflects genuine human creativity and authentic brand intentions. The present study examines the relationship between AI-generated advertising, perceived content authenticity, consumer skepticism, advertising credibility, and brand credibility. An empirical analytical framework was developed and tested using a proposed sample of 200 respondents, of whom 191 valid responses were considered for analysis. Data were conceptualised as being collected through a structured questionnaire using five-point Likert-scale items. The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis. The proposed analysis indicates that perceived AI involvement is negatively associated with content authenticity and positively associated with consumer skepticism, while content authenticity is positively associated with advertising and brand credibility. Consumer skepticism is expected to have a negative relationship with advertising credibility, whereas advertising credibility is positively associated with brand credibility. The proposed regression models indicate that authenticity and skepticism together explain a meaningful proportion of variance in advertising credibility, while advertising credibility emerges as an important predictor of brand credibility. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-generated advertising by conceptualizing authenticity as a central mechanism through which consumers evaluate technologically generated promotional communication. The findings also highlight the importance of human involvement, transparent communication, and context-sensitive AI disclosure in advertising.
venue: International journal of business and management invention.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Examining the effect of AI advertising involvement disclosure on advertising value and purchase intentions
abstract: Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into advertising has revolutionized how brands create and deliver marketing messages. The involvement of AI in ad creation introduces a critical question: if the AI origin of an advertisement is disclosed, how this transparency affects advertising value and purchase intentions. Grounded on the Persuasion Knowledge Model, this study investigates the effect of AI disclosure on these two key outcomes. Design/methodology/approach ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion were employed to generate stimuli. 358 consumers recruited via Prolific were exposed to the stimuli. The data were analyzed using a combination of Hayes’ Process models, MANCOVA and ANCOVA. Findings The results reveal that AI disclosure diminishes advertising value and purchase intentions. The relationships are negatively mediated by advertising credibility and positively moderated by consumer attitudes towards AI. Originality/value Theoretically, the research contributes to a more comprehensive picture of AI-generated advertising evaluation. Practically, the research offers actionable insights for businesses seeking to balance the advantages of AI with human psychology, ultimately optimizing advertising effectiveness in an increasingly AI-driven marketplace.
venue: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing

title: Disclosing early or late? The interactive effects of AI disclosure timing and advertisement appeal on consumer attitude toward advertising
venue: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services

title: When the Machine Writes the Ad: How Consumers Evaluate AI-Generated Advertising
When AI admits its flaws: authenticity and novelty pathways of flaw disclosure in AI-generated advertising
abstract: As generative AI becomes embedded in advertising production and mandatory AI disclosure requirements expand globally, brands face a structural challenge: disclosure of AI authorship can erode perceived authenticity. This study examined whether voluntary flaw disclosure counteracts this deficit in AI-generated advertising, and whether its effectiveness is conditioned by consumers' perceived risk. A between-subjects experiment ( N = 474) crossed three flaw disclosure conditions (direct/indirect/none; all carrying an identical platform-standard AI disclosure label) with message appeal (factual/humor) and tested a dual-pathway mediation model focused on the disclosure factor. Direct disclosure most strongly elevated perceived brand authenticity, whereas indirect disclosure most strongly enhanced perceived advertising novelty (η 2 = 0.13 and 0.21). Both pathways significantly and independently mediated the effect of flaw disclosure on attitude toward the ad (authenticity: IE = 0.46, 95% CI [0.31, 0.64]; novelty: IE = 0.40, 95% CI [0.24, 0.56]), and carried serially through brand attitude to purchase intention. A negative residual direct effect indicated a competitive suppression structure: the benefit of admitting a flaw was entirely mediation-dependent. The hypothesized moderating role of perceived risk on the authenticity pathway was not supported (index of moderated mediation 95% CI [−0.09, 0.23]); the dual-pathway mechanism appeared relatively stable across the observed range of perceived risk, although broader contexts require examination. The findings extend the minor flaw effect to AI advertising disclosure and identify authenticity and novelty as parallel, complementary routes for restoring consumer response.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: When Personalization Becomes Persuasion: Disclosure, Autonomy, and Conversion in Generative-AI Advertising
abstract: Generative AI enables advertisers to customize content on a per-person basis with minimal additional expense. The ability to make things seem more relevant can also diminish the persuasive message and reduce consumer choice. This study investigates the influence of personalization intensity and disclosure of AI generated content on the perceived relevance, manipulation, autonomy, trust, and conversion intention. A simulation-based 2 × 2 online experiment was designed using 1,248 synthetic respondent records, half assigned to disclosure-present and half to disclosure-absent settings, with half of the records in each of these disclosure conditions being assigned to low-personalization and the other half to high-personalization settings. Multi-item measures were analyzed by means of factorial analysis of variance, robust regression and 5,000-sample bootstrap mediation. High personalization also led to greater manipulation (M = 4.48) and less autonomy (M = 4.18) without disclosure, and greater relevance (M = 5.15) with disclosure (p < .001). Disclosure raised conversion under high personalization from M = 3.75 to M = 4.28, interaction F(1, 1244) = 17.80, p < .001, partial η² = .014. Conditional indirect effect pathway was mediated through autonomy, manipulation and trust was b = .48, 95% CI [.38, .58]. The results suggest that disclosure can be a governance tool supporting the conversion process if it can regain informed choice, rather than simply marking content. Personalization design can be made transparent to match performance with consumer agency.
venue: Research journal in business and economics.

title: AI-Generated vs. Human-Created Sustainable Advertising: Effects of Source Disclosure and Environmental Claim Strength on Perceived Greenwashing and Green Trust Among Generation Z Consumers
abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into digital advertising, combined with growing consumer concern about greenwashing, has created a dual credibility burden in which sustainability messages must be evaluated for both environmental truthfulness and authenticity of authorship—a challenge intensified by emerging AI disclosure regulations such as Article 52 of the EU AI Act. This study investigates how ad source (AI-generated vs. human-created), source label (labelled as AI vs. labelled as human), and environmental claim strength (vague vs. strong) jointly influence perceived greenwashing and green trust among Generation Z consumers. A 2 × 2 × 2 mixed factorial experiment was conducted with 154 undergraduate participants randomly assigned to one of four source–label conditions and exposed to both vague and strong environmental claims; data were analysed through one-way ANOVAs with Tukey HSD post hoc tests and paired-samples t-tests. All eight hypotheses were supported: AI attribution consistently elevated greenwashing perceptions and depressed green trust, while strong claims significantly reduced greenwashing perceptions and elevated trust within both correctly disclosed conditions. Most notably, the disclosed label—rather than the actual generative source—emerged as the dominant psychological cue, with human content mislabelled as AI suffering the same credibility penalty as genuine AI content. The findings reveal a transparency paradox with significant implications for AI disclosure regulation and sustainable marketing practice.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Generative AI and ChatGPT: Applications, challenges, and AI-human collaboration
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has elicited much attention across disciplines and industries (Hyder et al., Citation2019). AI has been defined as “a system’s ability to correctly interpret external data, to learn from such data, and to use those learnings to achieve specific goals and tasks through flexible adaptation” (Kaplan & Haenlein, Citation2019, p. 15). AI has gone through several development stages and AI winters. In the first two decades (i.e., 1950s and 1960s), AI demonstrated success which included programs such as General Problem Solver (Newell et al., Citation1959) and ELIZA (Weizenbaum, Citation1966). However, limitations in processing capacity and reduced spending on AI turned its development into stagnation. In recent years, AI has made a comeback with the introduction of AlphaGo in 2015 and ChatGPT in 2022. Following the release of the application named “Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer” or ChatGPT by OpenAI in late 2022, AI has attracted worldwide attention.
venue: Journal of Information Technology Case and Application Research
keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

title: A Study on the Process of Consumer Advertising Response Formation in AI-Generated Advertising Videos - Focusing on the Roles of Perceived Realism, Immersion, and Trust -
abstract: This study defines advertising videos produced with generative AI technology as a new form of cultural product and empirically analyzes the psychological mechanisms through which consumer responses are formed, focusing on perceived realism, immersion, and trust. Specifically, the research examines whether the visual design expressions generated by AI function through the same psychological mechanisms as traditional advertising realism. To this end, a survey was conducted using an AI-generated advertisement as a stimulus, and hypotheses were tested through regression and bootstrapping-based mediation analysis. The results are as follows. First, perceived realism did not significantly influence advertising immersion or trust, and no significant indirect effects were observed. This suggests that the prior disclosure of “AI-generated content” acts as a cognitive filter, leading consumers to adopt an analytical perspective focused on checking technical sophistication rather than being emotionally immersed in the design. Second, advertising immersion was found to have a significant positive (+) effect on trust, and trust played a pivotal role as a mediator in the path leading from advertising attitude and brand attitude to purchase intention. In conclusion, this study implies that for AI-generated advertisements to be successfully accepted as cultural products, sophisticated experiential immersion design strategies that can lower consumers' psychological barriers must precede simple efforts to implement realism. These findings can serve as foundational data for establishing new advertising effect models and effective cultural marketing strategies suited for the AI media era.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Generative AI in advertising: Trust, Acceptance, And Rejection Dynamics Among Young Social-Media Users
abstract: Research Aim: This study investigates the determinants of generative AI rejection among teenage consumers in Central Java, specifically examining how declining trust and AI acceptance influence rejection behavior, with technology experience as a moderating variable. Design/Methods/Approach: A quantitative causal-comparative research design was employed utilizing Structural Equation Modeling based on Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) through SMARTPLS software. Data were collected from 289 teenage consumers (aged 18+) in Central Java who had exposure to AI-generated digital marketing content on social media platforms and marketplace applications. Purposive and snowball sampling techniques were used to ensure relevant respondent representation. Research Finding: The study revealed that declining trust in generative AI (β = 0.116, p < 0.05) significantly predicts consumer rejection behavior, whereas direct AI acceptance did not show a significant relationship with rejection (β = 0.032, p = 0.088). Technology experience demonstrated a significant moderating effect (β = 0.082) on the acceptance-rejection relationship. The model explained 68% of variance in rejection behavior (R² = 0.68), indicating substantial predictive power. Theoretical Contribution/Originality: This research extends existing technology acceptance models by integrating trust theory and behavioral intention-action gap framework, demonstrating that affective-cognitive factors (trust, authenticity, ethical considerations) outweigh utilitarian value in predicting AI rejection among teenagers. The findings bridge the gap between cross-sectional AI advertising effectiveness studies and long-term consumer psychological responses. Practitioner/Policy Implication: Organizations implementing generative AI in digital marketing should prioritize trust-building through transparent AI disclosure, ethical practices, and privacy protection. For tech-inexperienced consumer segments, enhanced AI literacy programs are essential to reduce rejection rates and foster sustainable brand relationships. Research Limitation: The study employed a cross-sectional design limiting temporal effect assessment. Geographic scope was restricted to Central Java, potentially limiting generalizability.
