Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs and additional variables such as AI literacy, innovation orientation, and negative technology experiences.

title: How the Use of AI-Generated Advertising Affects Generation Z Consumers' Brand Trust and Purchase Intentions
abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers a great means to produce advertising copy, images, and videos rapidly, continuously, and at scale, its effectiveness is contingent on consumers' perceptions of the human and the human processes that influence the creation of the ads. It aims to grasp the extent to which the AI-generated advertisements can impact the purchase intent and brand trust of Generation Z consumers. It discusses the difference between results from AI-generated ad copy and identifying the fact that the copy was created with artificial intelligence, as well as combining data from advertisement experiments, canvassing, social media research, and a Generation Z survey (with varying samples and outcomes). Research in the literature indicates that the 'fitness', authenticity, credibility, and interpretation of disclosure are more effective in determining responses than sole AI authorship. One of the most likely courses to achieve the intention to buy, and one that few studies address with an eye on Generation Z, is trust. The recommendations of the review are a holistic approach, the consideration of threshold effects of causality, as well as transparent and correct advertising, not only with regard to advertising but also to show clear responsibility of the human being.
venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Anthropomorphism and transparency interplay on consumer behaviour in generative AI-driven marketing communication
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the impact of Generative AI (GAI)-produced marketing communication on consumer trust and behavioural intentions, particularly purchase intention. This study explores how GAI’s anthropomorphism and transparency influence these outcomes. The findings aim to expand existing research and provide actionable guidance for integrating GAI into practical marketing strategies. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 444 participants was recruited through Prolific to complete a survey based on different types of marketing contexts. Then, the dataset created through the survey data is analysed using statistical analysis to test the impact of the anthropomorphism of GAI on consumer behaviour in two marketing communication scenarios: chatbots and promotion advertisements (posters). Findings Anthropomorphism enhances purchase intention directly and indirectly through perceived social presence and trust. Transparency, i.e., the disclosure of AI-generated content, weakens the effect of anthropomorphism on social presence, decreasing the impact as transparency increases. Marketing scenarios (chatbot vs poster) influence the strength of these effects, with chatbots amplifying the mediating role of social presence and trust. However, the overall mediation mechanism linking anthropomorphism to purchase intention through social presence and trust remains stable across different communication scenarios and levels of transparency. Originality/value Few studies have comprehensively explored the impact and mechanisms of GAI on multi-faceted consumer behaviour intentions. This study provides new insights and findings on applying anthropomorphic GAI in marketing communication.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Risk-Calibrated Generative AI Governance for Responsible AI Adoption in U.S. Organizations: Evidence from Marketing and Corporate Disclosures
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in marketing content creation, personalization, customer communication, advertising, and multi-channel campaign execution. Although GenAI can improve speed and scalability, its use creates risks involving accuracy, privacy, intellectual property, bias, compliance, brand consistency, and consumer protection. This study develops and empirically examines a risk-calibrated governance framework for cross-functional marketing projects. The research combines an integrative review and thematic synthesis of relevant scholarly literature with an archival content analysis of official AI-governance disclosures from a purposive sample of large U.S. public companies across technology, finance, and consumer/media sectors. Six governance gates were coded as publicly disclosed or not observed: risk classification, input and data governance, output quality review, legal and ethical compliance, approval and human oversight, and post-deployment monitoring and escalation. The mean governance disclosure score was 5.27 out of 6. Legal and ethical compliance was universally disclosed within the sample, while data governance, risk classification, output quality review, and approval or human oversight were also widely observed. Post-deployment monitoring and escalation was the least consistently disclosed governance stage. Fisher's exact test showed that firms disclosing risk classification were more likely to disclose approval or human-oversight controls (odds ratio = 36.00, p = .038). The corresponding association between risk classification and post-deployment monitoring was positive but not statistically significant (odds ratio = 10.67, p = .117). Governance disclosure scores did not differ significantly across sectors (Kruskal-Wallis H = 0.067, p = .967). The findings support risk-calibrated pre-deployment oversight while highlighting comparatively less consistent public disclosure of lifecycle monitoring after deployment
venue: Journal of Economics Finance and Accounting Studies
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: When the Brand Is No Longer Human: Generative AI, Perceived Human Agency and the Future of Consumer-Brand Relationships
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is moving rapidly from a backstage marketing technology to a visible creator of advertisements, social-media content, brand stories, synthetic models and conversational communication. This transition raises a fundamental branding question: what happens to consumer-brand relationships when consumers perceive that meaningful communicative agency has shifted from humans to machines? Existing research documents consumer responses to AI-authored messages, AI disclosures, virtual influencers and synthetic advertising, but these streams remain fragmented and frequently emphasise immediate outcomes such as advertising attitudes, purchase intentions or credibility. This conceptual study integrates consumer-brand relationship theory, anthropomorphism and mind-perception research, brand-authenticity scholarship and emerging GenAI-marketing evidence to explain the relational consequences of AI-generated brand communication. It introduces perceived human agency as a central mechanism and develops an AI-Humanity Paradox: GenAI can simultaneously increase perceived innovativeness, novelty and creative capability while weakening brand humanness, authenticity and emotional sincerity. Comparative evidence from Coca-Cola's GenAI-generated Holidays Are Coming campaign and Levi's collaboration with Lalaland.ai demonstrates how these tensions become particularly salient when AI enters communication domains associated with heritage, emotion, identity and human representation. The paper further distinguishes AI-assisted from AI-authored communication and proposes that perceived replacement of human intention, rather than AI use per se, determines relational risk. The resulting framework contributes to emerging research on GenAI and branding by repositioning artificial content generation as a problem of agency attribution, authenticity and relationship meaning.
venue: Stallion Journal for Multidisciplinary Associated Research Studies
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: A Study of the Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Generated Image Advertising and Consumer Brand Awareness
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence technology is bringing tremendous changes to the advertising industry.Currently, there is relatively little research on the relationship between AI image advertising and consumer brand awareness.Based on the brand equity theory, this study constructed two theoretical models, "quality to brand awareness" and "acceptance willingness to brand awareness" and conducted experimental research by analyzing data from 419 questionnaires from China online respondents.The experimental data shows that 73.5% of the respondents believed that they had seen AI image advertisements, and 24.3% of the respondents suspected that they had seen AI image advertisements, this indicates that by the end of 2024, AI image ads have been widely exposed on the China Internet and have a high degree of recognizability even without the disclosure of AI labels.The research results show that the three dimensions of the quality of AI image advertisements in this paper, namely informativeness, entertainment, and credibility, all have a significant positive relationship with consumer brand awareness, and credibility has the strongest influence.There is a significant positive relationship between consumer willingness to accept AI image advertising and consumer brand awareness, and the influence is relatively strong.The researchers suggest that relevant practitioners should focus on enhancing the credibility of AI image ads when creating or using them, and on this basis improve the informativeness and entertainment of the ads.Based on the above findings, this paper contributes to the relevant literature on advertising communication, generative AI advertising, consumers, and brand awareness.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: From AI-Assisted to AI-Generated: A Systematic Review of AI Involvement Disclosure and Consumer Responses in Advertising
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has intensified the need to understand how disclosure of AI involvement influences consumer responses. This systematic literature review synthesizes empirical evidence on AI involvement disclosure in advertising, focusing on disclosure forms, consumer responses, psychological mechanisms, and contextual conditions. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, Scopus-indexed, English-language, peer-reviewed empirical studies published from 2022 to 2026 were considered for inclusion. After applying the predefined eligibility and journal-level selection criteria, 20 studies published from 2024 to 2026 constituted the final corpus. Methodological quality was considered using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), separately from the Journal Impact Factor used as a journal-level delimitation criterion. Seventeen of the 20 studies employed primary quantitative approaches, demonstrating the predominance of experimental, survey, and related quantitative designs. The synthesis indicates that consumer responses to AI disclosure are conditional rather than uniformly positive or negative. Disclosure was associated with variations in authenticity, credibility, trust, perceived effort, attitudes, engagement, and behavioral intentions, with these relationships shaped by psychological mechanisms and contextual factors such as perceived human involvement, disclosure format, advertising appeal, privacy concerns, and AI competency. The review contributes a mechanism-based understanding of AI disclosure by emphasizing a disclosure–interpretation–response process in which consumers interpret the role of AI and human involvement before forming advertising evaluations and behavioral responses. The findings highlight the importance of communicating not merely the presence of AI but also its specific role in advertising production and identify directions for more transparent and context-sensitive AI disclosure practices.

title: AI versus Human Advertising: Interview Analysis in Romania
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has brought key questions regarding brand image, emotional engagement and ethics. The purpose of this paper is to investigate marketing professionals’ perceptions regarding AI-generated marketing content (RGMC) in the Romanian context. With a qualitative approach, in-depth interviews were conducted to two senior marketing experts specialized in brand management and online marketing. The results indicate that rather than as a replacement for human creativity or strategic judgment, AI is seen as an augmentative tool to improve efficiency and scalability. Although AI-generated content can drive consumer engagement, its impact is mostly contingent on human control as well as brand maturity and audience nature. Ethics, transparency and AI disclosure, also represent interesting, investigated topics, in relation to trust and brand perception. Taken together, the study demonstrates the need of a blend model in which AI-powered efficiency meets human creativity and moral responsibility in advertising industry today.
venue: Proceedings of the ... International Conference on Business Excellence

title: The Era of AI-Generated Advertising: A Qualitative Study on Consumers' Perceptions of Authenticity in AI Advertising
abstract: Denna studie syftar att visa på kopplingar mellan konsumentåsikter mot generativ AI och undersöka fenomen såsom consumer resistance genom boycotting och andra konsumentdrivna initiativ mot företag som använder generativ AI. För att uppnå detta var tio individer intervjuade genom att använda elicitering i en semistrukturerad intervjumetod som vår huvudsakliga empiri. I intervjuerna var intervjupersonerna uppmuntrade att informera deras åsikter och personliga historia mot konceptet av generativ AI i reklam, och om AI reklamen var effektfull i att presentera en god produkt. Genom dessa intervjuer har denna studie dragit slutsatsen att intervjupersonerna kan delas upp i två grupper varav en av grupperna ansåg att reklamen förlorade sitt värde när intervjupersonen fick veta att den var AI genererad, och en grupp som inte ansåg att det var moraliskt fel att använda generativ AI i reklam. Båda dessa grupper tyckte att generativ AI är oetiskt och att faktumet att reklamen var AI genererad inte hjälpte kvaliteten av reklamen.
venue: Lund University Publications Student Papers (Lund University)
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: How generative AI Is shaping the future of marketing
abstract: Generative AI (Gen AI) is shaping the future of marketing. In the next decade, Gen AI will influence how marketers interact and communicate with customers, help create and deliver marketing content (text, images, and video), and inform methods for researching and developing new products and services. In both service and sales settings, Gen AI will affect customers directly and significantly. Therefore, marketers, researchers, and public policy makers require a clear understanding of Gen AI and its potential, as well as its limitations. To assist marketers in thinking through the adoption and implementation of Gen AI, the current article presents a four-quadrant organizing framework that highlights trade-offs in both the nature of Gen AI inputs and the extent of human augmentation needed to deliver Gen AI–generated outputs. This framework provides guidance for the selection and implementation of Gen AI tools, as well as recommendations for further research.
venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Consumer Attitude Towards AI-Generated Advertisement
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and its increasing integration in the advertising market have transformed both the deployment and creation of marketing content. Although AI-generated advertisements provide competitive advantages like cost efficiency, scalability and personalization but, the effectiveness ultimately depends on consumer perception and attitude. This study helps to understand consumer awareness of AI-generated advertisements, the stimulus-based responses before and after disclosure of AI involvement, it also analyzes perceived efficiency and overall attitude. Data was collected first handed through a structured online questionnaire. As the world is moving towards AI, the findings indicate high awareness of AI-generated advertising and favorable psychological-based evaluations prior to disclosure except for the shifts in perception, particularly in relation to trust and authenticity. Perceived efficiency was evaluated positively in terms of message clarity and communication effectiveness, though emotional resonance remained a consideration. Respondents preferred transparency and had the overall cautiously positive attitude toward AI-generated with acknowledging future growth prospects. The study emphasizes the fact that consumer perception and attitude are crucial factors in determining the effectiveness of advertising in technologically mediated environments.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AI Disclosure in Advertising: Visual Attention and Consumer Responses across Construal Levels
abstract: Disclosure that advertising content was created using artificial intelligence is becoming common, yet its effects on consumer processing remain poorly understood. Prior research has focused primarily on evaluative outcomes, overlooking how AI disclosure may influence visual attention during ad exposure. Drawing on Construal Level Theory, this study examines how AI disclosure shapes visual attention and consumer responses across different construal levels. Conceptualizing AI disclosure as a transparency cue in digital advertising systems, this study uses a laboratory eye-tracking experiment with Instagram-style advertisements. Visual attention was measured as total view duration on the model’s face and the advertised product. AI disclosure reduced attention to the model’s face and increased attention to the product, particularly among low-construal consumers. In contrast, AI disclosure lowered model attitude and purchase intention among high-construal consumers, with model attitude mediating this effect. These findings show that AI disclosure shapes both attentional and evaluative stages of advertising processing.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Consumer Perceptions of Sincerity and Human Oversight in AI-Generated Emotional Advertising: Red Bull Qualitative Dataset
abstract: This dataset supports the research study "Designing Human Oversight for AI-Generated Emotional Advertising: A Qualitative Study of Consumer Sincerity." The dataset examines how consumers perceive emotional sincerity in human-created and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-generated advertisements. It focuses on two Red Bull advertisements associated with the "Gives You Wings" message. The research corpus comprises 17 respondent-labelled documents containing 170 open-ended questionnaire answers in Indonesian. Respondents evaluated Advertisement A and Advertisement B before learning their stated production origins. Advertisement A was identified as human-created, while Advertisement B was identified as GenAI-generated. Subsequent questions explored changes in perception, familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its advertising capabilities, and expectations for human involvement. The analysis addresses four research questions concerning emotional sincerity cues, disclosure-related reassessment, consumer perceptions of GenAI, and human oversight responsibilities. The accompanying analytical materials include a provisional master coding structure with 23 subcodes, 353 first-pass coding assignments, cross-case matrices, word-tree concordances, and supporting visualizations. Initial rule-assisted coding was performed outside NVivo 14. The materials were organized to support further qualitative review and analysis in NVivo 14. The preliminary findings identify visible human effort, narrative credibility, emotional plausibility, and brand consistency as important sincerity cues. Responses to production-origin disclosure vary. Consumers recognize GenAI's visual capabilities but frequently question its emotional storytelling. Human involvement is emphasized in creative direction, narrative development, emotional evaluation, and final quality control. The dataset provides supporting material for examining consumer-informed human oversight requirements in GenAI emotional advertising. The findings are exploratory and do not establish causal relationships.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: TRANSPARENT TECHNOLOGY: EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF AI-GENERATED AD DISCLOSURE ON CONSUMER TRUST, AUTHENTICITY, AND PURCHASE INTENTION
abstract: This study investigates how disclosure of AI-generated advertising content influences consumer perceptions and behaviors in an increasingly AI-driven marketing landscape. Using a 2×2 experimental design that manipulates AI-generative ad disclosure (present versus absent) and beliefs about AI's capability (high versus low complexity tasks), we examine the effects on perceived authenticity, trust, and purchase intention. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) framework, we theorize that disclosure serves as a critical stimulus affecting internal evaluative processes and subsequent consumer responses. Findings may reveal that disclosure effects are significantly moderated by consumers' pre-existing beliefs about AI's capabilities to perform complex tasks. This research examines the impact of AI-generated ad disclosure, focusing on ad content creation, consumers' perceptions of trust and authenticity, and the subsequent effect on consumers' purchase intention. This study contributes to the AI advertising body of literature by investigating how consumers respond differently to AI-generated ad content disclosure. As these technologies become more widespread in advertising, understanding how AI disclosure affects consumer perceptions of authenticity, trust, and purchase intentions becomes essential for advertisers and policymakers to develop appropriate disclosure guidelines.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: AI-Generated Advertising Content and Consumer Persuasion: The Moderating Role of Disclosure, Perceived Authenticity, and Product Involvement
abstract: Abstract: Using a 2 (content origin) × 2 (disclosure) × 2 (product involvement) between-subjects factorial experiment with 384 urban Indian consumers, this study tests how algorithmic attribution, disclosure, and involvement jointly shape advertising persuasion. Algorithmically-attributed content reduced perceived authenticity and purchase intention relative to human-attributed content; disclosure amplified skepticism, particularly under high involvement. The three-way interaction on purchase intention was significant, with the lowest intention in the disclosed, algorithmic, high-involvement condition. Perceived authenticity partially mediated the content-origin effect, accounting for 55% of the total effect, and product involvement significantly moderated this mediation at the second stage. Keywords: AI-Generated Advertising, Disclosure, Perceived Authenticity, Product Involvement, Purchase Intention JEL Classification Number: M31, M37, O33
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The persuasion detection framework: an AI-based approach for identifying persuasion principles in digital advertising.
abstract: This thesis is focused on the development of an AI-based framework for detecting persuasion techniques in digital advertising assets (specifically from Meta Ads). Drawing on Robert Cialdini’s seven principles of influence (reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, and unity) the framework translates each principle into a set of observable visual and textual elements, enabling their systematic identification in image and video advertising assets. The dataset consists of several hundred of advertisements collected through the Meta Ads Library across three industry sectors selected for their differing use of persuasive strategies. Detection is performed using a few-shot prompt-based large language model (specifically Claude), with results validated against a manually coded sample and presented in a binary detection matrix. To conclude, the thesis also includes a generative experiment in which the framework is applied in reverse: AI is used to create advertising assets (exclusively images) incorporating predefined combinations of persuasion principles, testing the framework's potential for both analytical and creative tasks. By combining perspectives from digital humanities, persuasion theory, and computational methods, this research offers a scalable approach to auditing and generating persuasive content in social media advertising.
venue: Electronic Theses and Dissertations Repository (University of Pisa)

title: ChatGPT, AI Advertising, and Advertising Research and Education
Ads from automatons: Consumer perceptions of AI modality disclosures and the roles of AI experience and dispositional persuasion knowledge on advertising outcomes
abstract: Extant literature on consumer reactions to AI-generated advertising have focused on resulting perceptions of creativity, objectivity, and effectiveness in specific situations, often invoking situational persuasion knowledge as a framework to guide explanations of reactions. Though informative, this leaves a research gap with regard to other forms of persuasion knowledge, ad contexts, and advertising-relevant outcomes. Through an experimental approach and in response to platform-specific guidelines and proposed laws mandating disclosures of AI-generated content in advertising, the current study seeks to understand the interaction of dispositional persuasion knowledge, experience with AI tools, and trust in AI to better explain consumer reactions to online banner ad elements labeled as generated by AI. We find a general consumer ambivalence toward advertising disclosed as AI-generated vs. a non-AI-generated control (regardless of AI-generated modality), but also novel positive effects of dispositional persuasion knowledge, AI experience, and trust in AI with regard to specific advertising-focused dependent variables when the use of AI-generated text in ads is disclosed. Theoretical and practical takeaways for marketers are discussed.
venue: Journal of Global Scholars of Marketing Science

title: When understanding heightens response: AI literacy, anthropomorphic perception, and AI anxiety in consumer responses to AI-generated Advertising
Decoding AI-Generated Advertising: Consumer Responses, Advertising Outcomes, and Strategic Leverage
abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping the advertising landscape by increasing efficiency, streamlining workflows, and reducing costs, contributing to its growing adoption among practitioners. At the same time, the expanding use of AI-generated content has prompted AI disclosure policies and transparency requirements from governments and digital platforms, making AI involvement in marketing communication increasingly visible to consumers. Although AI offers substantial production advantages, consumers and practitioners often evaluate AI-generated content through fundamentally different priorities and standards. Consequently, understanding how consumers perceive and respond to AI-generated advertising, and how its effectiveness differs from human-created advertising, has become increasingly important for both scholars and practitioners. This chapter synthesizes the emerging body of empirical research on consumer responses to AI-generated advertising, with particular emphasis on experimental and quantitative studies that provide insight into causal relationships and findings with broader generalizability. Specifically, it examines whether AI-generated advertising produces favorable or unfavorable outcomes, the psychological mechanisms underlying these effects, and the contextual conditions under which negative responses may be strengthened, mitigated, or reversed. Organized around findings across commercial and philanthropic contexts, including cause-related marketing and prosocial campaigns, this chapter highlights how consumers interpret AI-related cues and how these interpretations shape persuasion outcomes. By integrating findings across contexts, this review provides theoretical insights into AI-mediated marketing communication, offers practical guidance for practitioners, and identifies key directions for future research.

title: When AI takes over advertising : A study on consumers’ perceptions of AI-generated advertising and its impact on attitudes and organizational legitimacy
abstract: In line with today’s rapid technological development, the conditions for advertising have changed. The rise of generative AI has had a significant impact on the advertising industry, while also provoking various reactions. This suggests that generative AI not only affects how advertising is created, but also how it is interpreted and valued by consumers. By combining the Persuasion Knowledge Model and legitimacy theory, this study aims to investigate how AI-generated advertising affects consumers’ attitudes, their interpretation of persuasion attempts, and companies’ perceived legitimacy. This knowledge is intended to contribute to insights that can help companies make informed decisions regarding the use of AI-generated advertising content. The study employs a qualitative research design consisting of focus groups and individual semi-structured interviews. The results show that participants generally reacted negatively to AI-generated advertising, which contributed to negative perceptions of the companies behind it. Furthermore, participants questioned the underlying intentions of the advertisements and showed an awareness of their persuasive strategies, indicating activation of persuasion knowledge. These findings indicate that AI-generated advertising can negatively affect perceptions of organizational legitimacy, although these perceptions vary depending on factors such as industry and company size. Overall, these findings suggest that consumer attitudes are shaped not only by the technology itself, but also by how it is used and in what context. Given this, the study contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between AI-generated advertising, consumer attitudes and organizational legitimacy.

title: The Impact of AI-Generated Advertising on Consumer Trust and Brand Credibility
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged to create advertising text, graphics, videos, virtual representatives, product descriptions and personalized advertisements. While these applications can boost production efficiency and support quick experimentation, they also pose key challenges regarding authenticity, transparency, consumer trust, and brand credibility. The present study aims to explore the connections of the quality, transparency, authenticity, consumer trust and brand credibility with the perceived advertising quality of AI-generated advertisements in Pakistan. Based on the theories of source credibility, the Persuasion Knowledge Model and trust and signalling, a conceptual model is formulated for further exploration. A quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational research design is used, and all five constructs are measured by five-point Likert scales. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression are used in the analysis. The analysis results showed good internal consistency for each of the five constructs, ranging from .826 to .853 for Cronbach's alpha coefficient. Together, the three-advertising quality, transparency, and authenticity explain 38.5% of the variance in consumer trust. In addition, although consumer trust, advertising quality, and advertising authenticity show statistically significant positive relationship with brand credibility, transparency does not make a unique contribution after the other predictors are taken into account. The results underscore the need to consider relationships between the characteristics of AI-generated ads and the evaluations of their consumers. The study highlights the importance of transparent communication and the need for factual accuracy, human oversight, and verified advertising claims in responsible AI-driven marketing. The relationships between disclosure of AI and consumer trust and brand credibility should be explored with validated measurement instruments, systematic sampling, and experimental designs for future research to determine the relationship between the two. title: Preparing for an Era of Deepfakes and AI-Generated Ads: A Framework for Understanding Responses to Manipulated Advertising
abstract: Traditionally, the production and distribution of advertising material has relied on human effort and analog tools. However, technological innovations have given the advertising industry digital and automatic tools that enable advertisers to automate many advertising processes and produce “synthetic ads,” or ads comprising content based on the artificial and automatic production and modification of data. The emerging practice of synthetic advertising, to date the most sophisticated form of ad manipulation, relies on various artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, such as deepfakes and generative adversarial networks (GANs), to automatically create content that depicts an unreal, albeit convincing, artificial version of reality. In this article, a general framework is constructed to better understand how consumers respond to all forms of ad manipulation. It is anticipated that this article will help explain how consumers respond to the more sophisticated forms of synthetic ads—such as deepfakes—that are emerging at an accelerating rate. To guide research in this area, a research agenda is developed focusing on three manipulated advertising areas: ad falsity, consumer response, and originality. Furthermore, the implications for theory and industry are considered.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: Consumer Trust in AI-Generated Advertisements. A Comparative Study of AI and Human-Created Advertising Content
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence in advertising has created pressing questions about whether consumers can or will trust content they know a machine has crafted. This study examined how 412 adult consumers evaluated AI-generated versus human-created advertisements across six product sectors, investigating the mechanisms of perceived authenticity, cognitive engagement, and emotional response as mediators, and AI literacy as a boundary condition. Using a mixed experimental-survey design followed by structural equation modelling, mediation analysis, and cluster analysis, results showed that AI-generated advertisements received significantly lower trust ratings (d = 0.89), yet this gap narrowed substantially among participants with higher AI literacy. Perceived authenticity emerged as the strongest mediator, accounting for 31.2% of the indirect effect. Importantly, trust in AI advertising increased with repeated exposure, suggesting that familiarity attenuates initial scepticism. These findings yield actionable implications for practitioners and advance theoretical understanding of technology-mediated persuasion.
venue: COMMUSTY Journal of Communication Studies and Society

title: Signal competition in AI-generated retail advertising: Credibility, eeriness, and trust formation
abstract: Artificial intelligence generated advertising is widely adopted in retailing and consumer services, yet its effects on trust, engagement, and purchase intention remain theoretically inconsistent. This study addresses this anomaly by reconceptualising advertising effectiveness under algorithmic authorship as a process of signal resolution rather than additive persuasion. Drawing on signalling theory and advertising value theory, the study specifies advertising value as a formative signal system composed of informativeness, entertainment, and executional credibility, which simultaneously activates competing inferential pathways of perceived credibility and perceived eeriness. Using a theory-driven PLS-SEM model estimated on a quota-based U.S. consumer sample (N = 412), the results provide associative evidence of systematic asymmetry and suppression effects: identical executional cues strengthen credibility while concurrently amplifying eeriness, with trust patterns consistent with the relative dominance of these opposing inferences rather than from overall message quality. Trust functions as a conditional transmission mechanism to engagement and purchase intention, and AI disclosure is associated with shifts in signal weighting by attenuating credibility-based pathways and amplifying eeriness-based suppression. By identifying signal competition as a structural feature associated with AI-generated advertising, the study extends current theoretical understanding of algorithmic persuasion by introducing signal competition as a structural feature associated with AI-generated advertising, departing from human-centric models and clarifying why creative AI execution often fails to yield behavioural conversion.

title: Multimodal intertextuality and persuasion in advertising discourse
abstract: This paper provides an integrated social semiotic framework for analyzing intertextuality in multimodal advertising discourse. Following the distinction between manifest intertextuality and interdiscursivity, our model entails the three interrelated components of explicating what the intertextual sources are, how they are constructed with multimodal resources, and how they interact with the promotional discourse. Analysis of 30 popular video advertisements shows the fundamental role of character voices and different social semiotic activities in achieving the purpose of promoting products and services. Through intertextual devices, the advertisements construct multiple identities, including authoritative and peer ones, to evoke different reading positions. In particular, the identity of middle-class urbanites sharing their experiences and values with the audience is dominant. The intertextual devices achieve promotional, relational, and entertainment functions, and the promotional function is realized through sharing, recreating, expounding, and reporting activities, while the recommending activities only occupy a very small portion of the screen time of the advertisements. The framework of multimodal intertextuality provides a useful lens for explicating the complex meaning-making resources, their communicative functions, and hidden ideologies in advertising discourse, which can further provide new insight into the social reality.

title: Inspired by AI, inspired to order: AI-generated food advertising and online food ordering behavior
abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how food is promoted on social media, yet it remains unclear whether, how and for whom AI-generated food advertising is associated with online food ordering. Anchored in the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework, this study examines how four features of AI-generated food advertising (informativeness, entertainment, irritation and credibility) relate to two inspiration states (inspired-by and inspired-to), which in turn relate to online food ordering behavior, and tests AI exposure and skepticism toward AI-generated food advertising as boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 783 Vietnamese social media users with prior exposure to food-related video advertising and online food ordering experience. The hypothesized model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. Findings Informativeness, entertainment, irritation and credibility were positively associated with both inspired-by and inspired-to, and both inspiration states were positively associated with self-reported online food ordering behavior. Notably, irritation was positively, rather than negatively, related to inspiration. Skepticism toward AI-generated food advertising weakened the inspired-by–behavior link, whereas AI exposure showed no significant moderating effect. Practical implications Marketers should combine informative, entertaining and credible AI-generated content with mechanisms that convert inspiration into ordering (e.g. in-ad ordering links and timely offers), and should mitigate consumer skepticism through transparent disclosure and accurate representations of food. Originality/value This study is among the first to link AI-generated food advertising to online food ordering behavior through the two-stage inspiration mechanism (inspired-by and inspired-to). It clarifies the stage-dependent role of skepticism toward AI-generated content as a boundary condition of AI-driven persuasion in the food context.

title: The potential of generative AI for personalized persuasion at scale
abstract: Matching the language or content of a message to the psychological profile of its recipient (known as "personalized persuasion") is widely considered to be one of the most effective messaging strategies. We demonstrate that the rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, could accelerate this influence by making personalized persuasion scalable. Across four studies (consisting of seven sub-studies; total N = 1788), we show that personalized messages crafted by ChatGPT exhibit significantly more influence than non-personalized messages. This was true across different domains of persuasion (e.g., marketing of consumer products, political appeals for climate action), psychological profiles (e.g., personality traits, political ideology, moral foundations), and when only providing the LLM with a single, short prompt naming or describing the targeted psychological dimension. Thus, our findings are among the first to demonstrate the potential for LLMs to automate, and thereby scale, the use of personalized persuasion in ways that enhance its effectiveness and efficiency. We discuss the implications for researchers, practitioners, and the general public.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Consumer Perception of AI-generated Characters in Advertising Visuals
abstract: This master's thesis examines how consumers on the Czech market perceive and evaluate AI-generated characters in advertising visuals. It focuses on consumers' ability to recognize these characters, the effect of these characters on the overall credibility of the advertisement, and attitudes toward their use. The theoretical part defines generative artificial intelligence and synthetic characters and draws on Social Presence Theory, the Persuasion Knowledge Model, Processing Fluency, and Uncanny Valley theory, together with the concepts of authenticity and trust in advertising. The practical part combines a quantitative survey (N=195 respondents) with eight in-depth interviews. For six advertising visuals, respondents classified the nature of the character and rated it on scales of trustworthiness, naturalness, and authenticity. Consumers recognize an AI- generated character with above-average accuracy (71.1%), relying mainly on an overall impression of unnaturalness rather than on specific details. The hypothesis that AI-generated characters have lower trustworthiness was confirmed with a large to very large effect. Attitudes toward their use are reserved, more sensitive in categories dependent on trust and more tolerant in categories associated with innovation. The qualitative interviews showed...
venue: Digital Repository (National Repository of Grey Literature)
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: The Psychological Impact of Language in Persuasion and Advertising
abstract: This paper explores the issues of language influencing psychology of advertising and the extent to which it influences consumer perception, attitudes and behavior. The research is conducted based on the interdisciplinary knowledge of marketing, psychology, and linguistics on understanding how some linguistic strategies such as appeal to emotion, framing, reconstruction, and involvement in the story make the messages persuasive. It used a mixed-method design, in which quantitative survey data were used to get the responses of 300 respondents and qualitative content analysis of adverts. The findings indicate that emotional language is the best predictor of purchase intention followed by narrative engagement, framing, and repetition among others with the total consumer decision making being proposed at 62 percent. The findings of the correlation also confirm that strong relations between linguistic strategies, consumer engagement and brand recall are present, as well as perceived risk reduction. The study supports the Elaboration Likelihood Model because it confirms that the central and the peripheral processes take place concurrently when responding to advertising language. Furthermore, the findings indicate the need of the culturally sensitive and ethically responsible communication in improving trust and long-term brand relationships. The theoretical contribution of this research in the study of language as a central tool of persuasion, and the practical implication of this process in developing more efficient and responsible advertising practices in the modern digital world, are not less significant.

title: More Than Saying “It's AI”: How Role Disclosure Transparency in AI‐Generated Ads Influences Persuasion
abstract: This research examines how AI role disclosure transparency—the consumers' subjective perception of how clearly and informatively an advertisement communicates the role that AI played in the ad creation process—influences consumer evaluation of AI‐generated ads via ad creation process credibility. A high level of perceived transparency enhances ad creation process credibility, which, in turn, leads to a more favorable attitude toward the ad (Study 1 and 2). In addition, the effectiveness of AI role disclosure transparency is also amplified under two conditions: when the disclosure motive is framed as reactive rather than proactive (Study 3) and the presence of a regulatory compliance signal (Study 4). This research advances current understanding of strategic disclosure in AI‐assisted advertising and provides actionable insights for optimizing consumer response to AI‐generated content. From a managerial perspective, it offers a decision‐making framework grounded in empirical findings to guide marketers on how best to communicate AI involvement in ad creation.

title: When AI personalisation becomes persuasive: the roles of trust and consumer response in digital advertising
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed digital advertising by enabling firms to deliver highly personalized, predictive, and context‑aware advertising experiences. While prior work shows that personalisation increases perceived relevance and effectiveness, most studies conceptualize personalisation primarily as a targeting capability and pay limited attention to its persuasive role and the boundary conditions under which it drives behavioural responses (Bleier & Eisenbeiss, 2015; Aguirre et al., 2015). Addressing this gap, this study develops an integrated framework to examine how AI‑driven personalisation dimensions shape perceived personalisation quality, persuasion, and purchase intention in digital advertising environments. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response model, the Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Trust Theory, the study conceptualizes AI‑driven personalisation as a multidimensional construct comprising relevance, accuracy, consumer control, timeliness, and contextual fit. Data from 401 consumers with prior experience of AI‑generated personalized advertisements on digital and social media platforms were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. The results show that all five personalisation dimensions significantly enhance perceived personalisation quality, with relevance and contextual fit exerting the strongest effects. Perceived personalisation quality strongly influences persuasion and purchase intention, and persuasion partially mediates the relationship between personalisation and purchase intention. Furthermore, trust in AI advertising significantly strengthens the positive effect of persuasion on purchase intention. These findings extend prior personalisation research by shifting the focus from personalisation as a technical feature to personalisation as a perceived quality that activates persuasive processing in AI advertising. They also add to recent AI advertising work by identifying trust in AI advertising as a key boundary condition that amplifies the behavioural impact of persuasive personalized messages. The study provides theoretical and managerial implications for designing AI‑driven advertising strategies that align personalisation quality, persuasion, and consumer trust.

title: Laughing at Bias: An Exploratory Study on Generation Z’s Persuasion and Skepticism Toward AI- vs. Human-Generated Sexist Humorous Ads
venue: Communications in computer and information science

title: An Experimental Model of Purchase Intention to AI-Generated Advertising Based on Perceived Disguise, Agency, and Falsity
abstract: This study examines how consumer perceptions shape responses to AI-generated advertising and purchase intention. Drawing on persuasion knowledge and trust perspectives, the model integrates AI Disguise, Perceived AI Agency, and Awareness of Falsity as antecedents, with Ad Credibility, Perceived Sincerity, and Attitude Toward the Advertisement as mediating mechanisms. Using a 2 × 3 between-subjects experiment with 350 respondents and PLS-SEM, the results show that AI Disguise positively influences credibility and sincerity, whereas Perceived AI Agency and Awareness of Falsity negatively affect both. Ad Credibility and Perceived Sincerity positively influence attitude, while Attitude Toward the Advertisement strongly predicts Purchase Intention (β = 0.572, p < .001). The hypothesized path from credibility to sincerity is not supported. The findings indicate that consumer responses depend more on perceived human-likeness, agency, and recognition of synthetic origin than on AI use alone.
venue: International Conference on Cyber and IT Service Management (CITSM)

title: Easing AI-advertising aversion: how leadership for the greater good buffers negative response to AI-generated ads
abstract: The advertising industry is being reshaped by artificial intelligence (AI), offering innovation and efficiency in ad creation but also triggering consumer scepticism. This research examines consumer perceptions of AI-generated ads and their impact on consumer brand perceptions, highlighting strategies to mitigate negative reactions. Specifically, the role of responsible leadership, or leadership for the greater good, is explored as a means to counter adverse effects. Through four studies, the findings reveal that signalling AI usage in advertising can heighten negative reactions, but brands perceived as committed to the greater good can mitigate these effects. By demonstrating responsible leadership, brands can reduce negative consumer responses and improve the acceptability and effectiveness of AI-generated ads. This research offers valuable insights into navigating the challenges of AI in advertising while fostering positive consumer engagement.
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs
abstract: Most traditional AI safety research views models as machines and centers on algorithm-focused attacks developed by security experts. As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly common and competent, non-expert users can also impose risks during daily interactions. Observing this, we shift the perspective, by treating LLMs as human-like communicators to examine the interplay between everyday language interaction and AI safety. Specifically, we study how to persuade LLMs to jailbreak them. First, we propose a persuasion taxonomy derived from decades of social science research. Then, we apply the taxonomy to automatically generate persuasive adversarial prompts (PAP) to jailbreak LLMs. Results show that persuasion significantly increases the jailbreak risk across all risk categories: PAP consistently achieves an attack success rate of over 92% on Llama-2-7b-Chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 in 10 trials, surpassing recent algorithm-focused attacks. On the defense side, we explore various mechanisms against PAP, find a significant gap in existing defenses, and advocate for more fundamental solutions for AI safety.
venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: The Impact of AI Generated Advertising Content on Consumer Buying Intention and Consumer Engagement
abstract: This Study explores the difference between human generated advertising content and the AI generated Advertising content and this research explore the impact on AI generated advertising content on consumer engagement and consumer buying behavior. Qualitative approach used to unveil the perception about AI Generated Advertising content in the perspective of Marketers and AI experts and answer that what is different in humanly created advertising content and Ai generated advertising content. This study elaborates the impact of AIGAC on brands sales volumes and competitive edges. Researcher conducted interviews of marketers and creative directors to explore the phenomenon in their expert opinion. The research work highlights the importance of this emerging tool in industry and its contribution in brand building process specially brand communication strategies. This study discusses the abilities and accuracy of AI in Advertising particularly when we talk about human feelings and emotions. Finally, consumer perception about AI also concluded this study. Researcher found AI generated advertising content more effective than the humanly generated advertising content for Consumer Engagements and Consumer Buying Behavior. AI create more balanced and vibrant combinations in creativity of ads. Researcher finds that AI generated Advertising content will boost sales due to its high appeal of creativity. This study will provide direction to the practitioners for their future strategies regarding brand building, brand communication and Sales strategies. Future researches can get guidelines for their thematic researches.

title: LLM-Generated Ads: From Personalization Parity to Persuasion Superiority
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable of generating persuasive content, understanding their effectiveness across different advertising strategies becomes critical. This paper presents a two-part investigation examining LLM-generated advertising through complementary lenses: (1) personality-based and (2) psychological persuasion principles. In our first study (n=400), we tested whether LLMs could generate personalized advertisements tailored to specific personality traits (openness and neuroticism) and how their performance compared to human experts. Results showed that LLM-generated ads achieved statistical parity with human-written ads (51.1% vs. 48.9%, p > 0.05), with no significant performance differences for matched personalities. Building on these insights, our second study (n=800) shifted focus from individual personalization to universal persuasion, testing LLM performance across four foundational psychological principles: authority, consensus, cognition, and scarcity. AI-generated ads significantly outperformed human-created content, achieving a 59.1% preference rate (vs. 40.9%, p < 0.001), with the strongest performance in authority (63.0%) and consensus (62.5%) appeals. Qualitative analysis revealed AI's advantage stems from crafting more sophisticated, aspirational messages and achieving superior visual-narrative coherence. Critically, this quality advantage proved robust: even after applying a 21.2 percentage point detection penalty when participants correctly identified AI-origin, AI ads still outperformed human ads, and 29.4% of participants chose AI content despite knowing its origin. These findings demonstrate LLMs' evolution from parity in personalization to superiority in persuasive storytelling, with significant implications for advertising practice given LLMs' near-zero marginal cost and time requirements compared to human experts.

title: Disclosing AI-generated image or copy? Understanding consumer responses to the AI-generated green advertisements
keywords: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

title: AI-Generated Persuasion in Conflict: A Study of Israeli Influencers’ Perspective
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in social media production and circulation, creating new opportunities for persuasive communication while also intensifying concerns about authenticity, manipulation, and misinformation during conflict. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with eight Israeli social media influencers from different content domains who posted war-related content in the first months of the Israel-Gaza war. Across interviews, AI was framed as an amplifier of emotion, narrative clarity, and virality, but also as a tool that can blur the boundary between persuasion and propaganda. Ethical evaluations were frequently shaped by political alignment, and almost all participants supported stronger transparency-oriented safeguards such as labeling or watermarking, even while questioning their feasibility. The findings position influencers as emerging gatekeepers in conflict communication and illustrate how AI intensifies both expressive capacity and credibility dilemmas. Given the small, context-specific sample and the reliance on self-reported accounts, the study offers exploratory rather than generalizable conclusions, and points to the need for further comparative research and governance frameworks that combine platform accountability with public media literacy.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Artificial Influence: An Analysis Of AI-Driven Persuasion
abstract: Persuasion is a key aspect of what it means to be human, and is central to business, politics, and other endeavors. Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have produced AI systems that are capable of persuading humans to buy products, watch videos, click on search results, and more. Even systems that are not explicitly designed to persuade may do so in practice. In the future, increasingly anthropomorphic AI systems may form ongoing relationships with users, increasing their persuasive power. This paper investigates the uncertain future of persuasive AI systems. We examine ways that AI could qualitatively alter our relationship to and views regarding persuasion by shifting the balance of persuasive power, allowing personalized persuasion to be deployed at scale, powering misinformation campaigns, and changing the way humans can shape their own discourse. We consider ways AI-driven persuasion could differ from human-driven persuasion. We warn that ubiquitous highlypersuasive AI systems could alter our information environment so significantly so as to contribute to a loss of human control of our own future. In response, we examine several potential responses to AI-driven persuasion: prohibition, identification of AI agents, truthful AI, and legal remedies. We conclude that none of these solutions will be airtight, and that individuals and governments will need to take active steps to guard against the most pernicious effects of persuasive AI.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Who’s Liable When AI Misleads? Legal Accountability in AI-Generated Advertising.
abstract: This project investigates the legal and policy challenges surrounding AI-generated advertising and accountability. As companies increasingly use AI tools to create images, videos, and even synthetic influencers, questions arise about who should be held responsible when these ads mislead consumers. Current laws in the U.S. and abroad were written for human advertisers, leaving gaps around the roles of AI providers, platforms, and virtual influencers. This research explores these gaps through a comparative lens, looking at how jurisdictions such as the UK and EU regulate disclosure, child protection, and platform responsibility. Her final paper will propose concrete policy recommendations, such as clearer disclosure rules, updated protections for children, and possible shared liability models, to ensure AI advertising is transparent, trustworthy, and fair.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Central and peripheral routes in the age of AI: replicating and extending the elaboration likelihood model in advertising
The Risks of AI-Generated, Hyper-Personalized Digital Advertisements
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: Legal Persuasion in the Age of AI
abstract: This article examines algorithmic persuasion within a long-term theoretical framework that links language, persuasion, and legal rationality. Beginning with the classical relationship between speech, corporeality, and persuasion, the analysis traces the historical process through which language becomes progressively objectified, culminating in contemporary generative artificial intelligence. The paper distinguishes persuasion as a psychological effect from persuasiveness as the quality of a discourse as rational achievement emerging in oppositional argumentative contexts, a distinction central to modern legal theory. Drawing on recent empirical literature, the article shows that generative AI can reach persuasive effectiveness comparable to human agents, while identifying transparency, personalization, and cultural heuristics as key moderating factors. Finally, it highlights the ethical and juridical tensions between technological efficiency, human oversight, privacy, and the preservation of human dignity.
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: AI VERSUS HUMAN-CREATED FOOD ADVERTISEMENTS: HOW APPEAL TYPES AND PERSUASION KNOWLEDGE SKEPTICISM DRIVE PURCHASE INTENTIONS
abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in the food and beverage industry is a growing phenomenon that is generating complex consumer responses, particularly the requirement to disclose any foods and beverages created with AI assistance. This study examines the interaction between the declared identity of an advertising creator (AI-generated versus human-created) and specific advertising appeals (nutritional versus taste) to determine their impacts on consumer purchase intentions, based on the Mind Perception Theory and the Persuasion Knowledge Model. In order to test the hypotheses, the 2 x 2 between subject experimental design was carried out, using the stimulus product of sugarcane juice, consisting of 320 participants. ANOVA and moderated mediation modeling (Model 8) in the SPSS PROCESS macro were employed to analyze the data, while controlling for the baseline health consciousness and attitudes toward AI. The results showed that there is a highly significant interaction between advertising creator and advertising appeal. Advertisements created by artificial intelligence, combined with a nutrition message, resulted in significantly increased purchase intention and reduced skepticism. Human-made ads, on the other hand, were much more effective when using a hedonic, taste appeal. Furthermore, the moderated mediation analysis confirmed that persuasion knowledge skepticism fully mediates this relationship. A cognitive mismatch happens when an AI promotes sensory taste, and when a human promotes strictly objective nutritional data – both lead to consumer skepticism and ultimately reducing purchase intention. This cognition resistance can be effectively reduced however, if AI is used in a way that matches its perceived computational agency with nutrition claims, or the human experiential capacity with sensory taste claims. Theoretically, this research offers insights that fully explain algorithm aversion in the context of food marketing. Practitioners get actionable guidelines, showing that the disclosure of AI authorship is not necessarily harmful. However, AI can serve as a valuable marketing tool when it is skillfully paired with compelling, data-driven claims, and human touch is still crucial for substantiating sensory and emotional claims.
venue: Insights (Bhalwal) International Journal of Humanities Management and Social Sciences

title: Digital Influence, Creator Economies and Communication Ethics: A Conceptual Model of Persuasion, Disclosure and Accountability in AI-Augmented Social Media Marketing
abstract: The creator economy has become a primary channel of commercial and political persuasion. Artificial intelligence is now changing it from two directions. Creators use generative tools to produce content at a scale and speed no human team could match, while brands deploy synthetic influencers who never existed and AI systems that can match persuasive messages to individual psychological profiles. This conceptual, non-empirical paper develops a model of communication ethics for AI-augmented influence. It draws on persuasion theory and advertising ethics, on the influencer-marketing and creator-economy literatures, and on peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and 2026 on virtual influencers, AI-generated advertising and algorithmic and psychological targeting. Every source was checked against its Crossref record and screened for retractions and corrections. The paper identifies three requirements that persuasion must meet to be ethically legitimate. The audience must be able to recognise it as persuasion, must be able to identify who is persuading, and must keep the capacity to evaluate the claim. AI augmentation threatens each requirement. Generated content blurs the boundary between commercial and organic material, synthetic personas obscure the persuader, and psychological targeting and persuasive generation at scale weaken evaluation. From this recognition–identification–evaluation framework, the paper derives six propositions on the conditions under which AI-augmented influence remains ethically legitimate and legally compliant. It argues that disclosure rules designed for human influencers are necessary but inadequate, because they address recognition while leaving identification and evaluation largely unprotected. Using Nigeria's fast-growing influencer market and its advertising, consumer-protection and data-protection regimes as the anchoring case, the paper proposes a layered framework of obligations for regulators, platforms, brands and agencies, and creators.
venue: IIAR Journal of Business Management and Entrepreneurship
keywords: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

title: AI-Generated Ads: A Framework for Understanding Responses to Manipulated Advertising
abstract: Analog tools and human labor have historically been used in the creation and distribution of advertising material. The advertising industry can now automate many advertising processes and create “synthetic ads,” or ads that contain content that is created artificially and automatically through data modification and production. This is made possible by technological advancements in the advertising sector. Using a variety of Artificial Intelligence (Al) techniques, including deep fakes and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), the growing practice of synthetic advertising, which is currently the most sophisticated form of ad manipulation, automatically generates content that presents an artificial, albeit convincing, version of reality. A broad framework is developed in this study to gain a better understanding of how consumers react to various types of ad manipulation and how they feel about more complex synthetic ad formats like deep fakes. An agenda for research in this field is created, with an emphasis on the areas of manipulated advertising: originality, consumer response, and ad falsity. Moreover, consideration is given to the implications for theory and industry.

title: The Impact Of AI-Generated Content Advertising On Social Media On Customer Engagement And Brand Building
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have rapidly evolved to create advertising content for social media platforms at a scale that was once impossible without human production in personalized, low-cost ways. This study provides a conceptual and literature-based analysis of the impact of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) advertising on customer engagement and brand building on social platforms. Reviewing 20 peer-reviewed published papers from MDPI, Taylor & Francis, and Springer outlets, the review draws together evidence on the characteristics of AIGC advertisements, consumer response to AIGC advertisements, and downstream effects on brand trust, brand loyalty, and brand advocacy. Given the conditions where personalization is high and the source of AI-generated content is not salient, the analysis suggests that AI-generated ads can be as attention-grabbing and engaging as human-created content and potentially even more so. However, a disclosure of AI involvement can diminish consumer trust, empathy, and purchase intent, which is driven by the activation of persuasion knowledge and algorithm aversion. The proposed framework, comparative tables, and five conceptual diagrams presented below illustrate the importance of disclosure transparency and personalization in increasing or decreasing the value of AIGC advertising as a mechanism to create lasting brand equity or just passing moments of engagement. The paper ends with a research agenda for researchers and practitioners working in this rapidly changing field, as well as limitations of the current evidence base.
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

title: AI-Generated Advertising: Impact on Trust, Purchase Likelihood, and Engagement
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into digital marketing, this study examined differences in trust, purchase likelihood, and emotional engagement between AI-generated and human-created advertisements. A survey of university students found no significant difference in trust. Human-created advertisements were more effective in driving purchase likelihood while AI-generated advertisements produced higher emotional engagement. These findings suggest that AI- and human-created content serve complementary roles in digital marketing strategies.
venue: Journal of Marketing Development and Competitiveness

title: THE POWER OF PERSUASION IN DIGITAL ADVERTISING: EXAMINING THE ELABORATION LIKELIHOOD MODEL
abstract: This paper explores central route processing in modern advertising, drawing on Petty and Cacioppo’s (1986) Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM). This study employs a qualitative research approach using in-depth interviews. Based on the study, central route processing occurs when consumers critically evaluate persuasive messages based on argument strength, particularly for high-involvement products such as automobiles and financial services. The digital advertising landscape, including e-commerce platforms, search engine ads, and personalized marketing, enhances central processing by providing extensive product information and comparisons. While peripheral route processing, driven by heuristics and emotional appeals, is dominant in social media advertising, central route processing fosters long-lasting, resistant, and behaviour-predictive attitudes. The interplay of both routes in dual processing strategies maximizes advertising effectiveness, ensuring engagement across diverse consumer segments. As technology evolves, advertisers must leverage central processing to build trust, brand loyalty, and informed decision-making. However, the limitations of the Elaborations Likelihood Model, including its binary distinction and contextual variability, highlight the need for a more nuanced understanding of consumer persuasion in the digital age.
venue: African Journal of Social and Behavioural Sciences

title: Testing theories of political persuasion using AI
abstract: Despite its importance to society and many decades of research, key questions about the social and psychological processes of political persuasion remain unanswered, often due to data limitations. We propose that AI tools, specifically generative large language models (LLMs), can be used to address these limitations, offering important advantages in the study of political persuasion. In two preregistered online survey experiments, we demonstrate the potential of generative AI as a tool to study persuasion and provide important insights about the psychological and communicative processes that lead to increased persuasion. Specifically, we test the effects of four AI-generated counterattitudinal persuasive strategies, designed to test the effectiveness of messages that include customization (writing messages based on a receiver's personal traits and beliefs), and elaboration (increased psychological engagement with the argument through interaction). We find that all four types of persuasive AI produce significant attitude change relative to the control and shift vote support for candidates espousing views consistent with the treatments. However, we do not find evidence that message customization via microtargeting or cognitive elaboration through interaction with the AI have much more persuasive effect than a single generic message. These findings have implications for different theories of persuasion, which we discuss. Finally, we find that although persuasive messages are able to moderate some people's attitudes, they have inconsistent and weaker effects on the democratic reciprocity people grant to their political opponents. This suggests that attitude moderation (ideological depolarization) does not necessarily lead to increased democratic tolerance or decreased affective polarization.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

title: AI-Generated Advertising Corpus: Ethos, Pathos, Logos Analysis Dataset — 50 Texts Across 5 Product Categories (GPT-3.5-turbo)
abstract: This dataset contains 50 advertising texts generated via the OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo API (April 2026) for computational rhetorical analysis. Texts span five product categories: Technology, Health, Finance, Luxury, and Sustainability (10 products per category). Each text was produced using a standardised prompt requesting persuasive advertising copy of 80-120 words for a general consumer audience, ensuring corpus comparability. The dataset is the primary empirical corpus for a study applying Aristotle's three rhetorical modes — Ethos, Pathos, Logos — as defined in the Rhetoric (335 BCE, I.2.1356a) to AI-generated marketing communication. The study investigates whether GPT-generated advertising copy conforms to, deviates from, or distorts the Aristotelian ideal of balanced rhetorical deployment, with implications for AI marketing ethics and consumer behaviour research. This work extends prior DBA research on AI's impact on Greek consumer behaviour (Aritzis, 2025, European International University Paris) into computational rhetoric and AI persuasion theory. Model used: gpt-3.5-turbo (OpenAI) Generation date: April 2026 Corpus size: 50 texts, average 113.4 words per text Total words: approximately 5,670 Analysis tool: Python 3.12, Google Colaboratory
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Synthetic Imagery and Brand Communication: A Semiotic Analysis of AI Visuals in Advertising
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly entered the visual production of advertising, transforming both the creative process and the symbolic language of brands. This article explores the emergence of AI-generated visuals in advertising campaigns through the lens of semiotics, aesthetics, and digital communication theory. By analyzing recent cases—such as Gucci’s experimental campaign featuring AI-generated models, Coca-Cola’s collaboration with generative platforms, Guess’s incorporation of AI visuals into fashion imagery, and Levi’s initiative to diversify representation through synthetic models—the study highlights how AI alters the codes of visual persuasion. The article situates AI visuals at the intersection of technological innovation and cultural meaning making, raising questions about authenticity, creativity, and the ethics of advertising. Drawing from semiotic theory, posthumanist aesthetics, and critical media studies, it argues that AI visuals constitute not merely a tool but a new visual paradigm in brand communication. While AI promises efficiency, personalization, and radical aesthetic novelty, it also produces tensions around originality, standardization, and consumer trust. The article concludes that AI visuals represent a hybrid form of cultural production, demanding new critical frameworks and ethical standards for the future of advertising. It also introduces an original analytical framework—the Post-Indexical Semiotics Model—to interpret how meaning, authorship, and authenticity are constructed in AI-generated advertising.
venue: The Journal of Communication and Media Studies

title: Visual persuasion in non-profit advertising : investigating the roles of emotional arousal, empathy and credibility for intentions to donate
abstract: For non-profit advertisers choosing the most persuasive image is an essential strategic decision to attract attention and donors. The effectiveness of a donation advertisement depends on the persuasiveness of the visual or visual persuasion. This doctoral dissertation focuses on investigating visual persuasion and its effects on intention to donate or prosocial behavior in non-profit advertising. Study 1 (re)introduces the concept of visual persuasion by providing an overview of past publications and proposing a concept explication for its use in the context of donor advertising. The central idea is that visual persuasion in donor advertising is conceptually divided into different levels: emotional arousal, empathy and credibility. This new concept explication is expected to enhance the understanding of visual persuasion in donor advertising by providing ways to approach and measure it, both by researchers and non-profit advertisers. Study 2 reveals a robust negative linear relationship between valence and arousal in non-profit ad images at an aggregate level and individual level, which is different from commercial ad images.
